#54541. Breaking: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

📅 11 Nov 2020 • ⏱️ 33m • 📚 Deep Dive (6666 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Bonappetit ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Best Cutting Boards for Slicing, Dicing, and Chopping (2026)

📅 11 Nov 2020 | ⏱️ 33 min read (6666 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~33 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop.
  • Latest in this update: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options.
  • A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A good cutting board is an essential kitchen tool that provides a layer of protection between your knife and your countertop. But the best cutting boards do more than just protect your counters during food prep—they provide a stable surface when you’re vigorously chopping and act as a protective surface that prevents prematurely dulling the blades of your kitchen knives. Cutting boards come in a variety of materials: plastic, wood, rubber, even glass and metal for inexplicable reasons. After testing dozens of boards of all sorts of materials over the course of six years, we have found five favorites. Read on to find out which might be best for you as well as how we tested and what we look for in the cutting boards we want to use every day.

Latest in this update: After much consideration and years of testing different boards, we decided to shift our top recommendations for wood boards to feature only end-grain options. They’re easier on knives and more beautiful to keep on the counter. And our new top pick is reasonably priced as end-grain boards go. For more on what makes end- and edge-grain boards different, click here. And if you’re looking for a quality (but truly inexpensive) wood board, we’d encourage you to look at these two Boos boards. They’re edge-grain, so they’ll wear your knives more quickly, but Boos makes almost universally great cutting boards.

Maple End-Grain Cutting Board (18" x 12").

A butcher block board from Texas’s Boardsmith won’t come cheap, but we think a large and sturdy wood cutting board is a worthy kitchen investment. A good wood cutting board can last decades and decades, and since it will likely live permanently on your counter, function as a key aesthetic component of your kitchen. Our editors have used this heavy-duty piece for over a year in their home kitchens, and even after daily use, it shows little to no wear and only minimal staining.

Sources indicate that what we love: The craftsmanship on the board is apparent as soon as you take it out of the box. The offset pattern of the individual pieces of wood is striking (as it is on most end-grain boards). And its construction feels smooth and solid.

In a recent development, as an end-grain board, it’s easy on knife blades, leaving them sharper than a less expensive edge-grain board. The real highlights, beyond the pure aesthetics, are in the small design features, though. Senior shopping editor Noah Kaufman has been using it in his home kitchen since June of 2025 and has found it the most stable board he’s ever used. That’s thanks to the addition of four grippy silicone-tipped feet on one side (you can order a Boardsmith without the feet, but you’d be giving away that stability). Those feet also raise the board up a little higher on the counter—which prevents the underside from retaining moisture and warping—and for Noah, they elevate the board to a very comfortable cutting height. It’s also reversible, with an effective, though not too deep, juice groove on the side of the footed side.

In a recent development, boardsmith’s end-grain boards are very customizable. They come in four sizes (we tested the 18" x 12" x 2", but the largest—24" x 18" x 2"—would make a beautiful always-out piece), three wood types (in addition to the maple, we tried walnut and cherry), and you can opt for features like juice and finger grooves. The feet are also optional, though they’re included by default, so you have to check a box if you want a board without feet.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: Again, this board is heavy, which makes it sturdy, but also a bit of a chore to clean. Because it’s wood, it also requires some upkeep in the form of oiling and buttering (the brand’s Board Butter has kept the surface of the Noah’s board in tip-top shape through months of use). Finally, while the feet are a vital feature, they do make the board a little less attractive if left on the counter with the juice groove facing up. But using the groove is a less frequent use than regular slicing and chopping, so you’ll be more likely to leave it feet side down—or at least turn it back over after you’re done cutting and cleaning.

In the long run: With long-term testing of a full year, the Boardsmith has stood up in a way that justifies its high price. It’s held on to minimal stains, and with a bit of oil and wax every three to four weeks, the board looks as beautiful as it did when it arrived.

R-Board Series Rectangular Wooden Maple Cutting Board, 18”x12”.

Boos boards, as they’re commonly called, are pretty much the gold standard for wood cutting boards, and this relatively affordable maple cutting board is a dream to cut on.

Recent findings suggest that what we love: Though maple is a hard wood, the cutting surface is smooth and has the perfect amount of give. In our testing, it seemed to almost embrace the knife blade with each chop. The board didn’t retain any food odors and it was easy to hand-wash (never put a wood board in the dishwasher!). Even beet juice disappeared after a good cleaning.

Recent findings suggest that boos Blocks come in many different sizes, we’ve found that the 18x12" size is just right for most home kitchens. This board is from the brand’s R-Board series, and it’s substantial without being too significant. There’s plenty of room to carve a roast chicken, but it’s small enough to slide into the cabinet where you keep your sheet pans (a half-sheet is 18x13") as long as you don’t have too much else in there. At 2.25" it’s the tallest (thickest) cutting board we tested, and it will add significant height to your cooking zone, which is something shorter home cooks should always keep in mind when choosing a chopping board.

What we’d leave: Though not necessarily a negative, this board is on the heavy side (10 lb.), and it does require frequent oiling to keep it in tip-top shape. Boos recommends their proprietary Mystery Oil and Board Cream, and if you buy directly from the brand, you can bundle the care products with the board.

What we love: Sonder’s board is beautiful, and like the Boardsmith, it features end-grain construction, which is easier on knives because they slide between the wood fibers, avoiding friction with the hard surface. End-grain boards also “self-heal,” which means that the fibers come back together after having been sliced—and I found that after rigorous use in a week of endless chopping tests, this board came out looking as beautiful as it had when it came out of the package. This board is made of American walnut and constructed in the US.

Sources indicate that the Sonder board also has some clever design elements: It’s hard to find an end-grain board that features a juice groove at this price point (the Boardsmith below, for example, costs almost $100 more). Flip the board over, and on the other side, it features three carved-out compartments, so you can slide chopped food to the side as you prep, keeping ingredients contained, separated, and out of the way. Those compartments can also be used for a fun charcuterie board setup: Use them to hold sauces and condiments or as a landing place for olive pits. Both sides of the board feature grippy rubber feet, and I found that this board stayed steady and level on the countertop even during heavy-duty chopping.

According to recent reports, this board was less cumbersome to take to the sink and hand wash than many of the large end-grain boards we tried. It has ergonomic handles carved into the sides, which makes for easy transport despite its heft and size. And because it’s a dark-colored wood, it reveals less sign of staining than other wooden boards.

In a recent development, what we’d leave: There’s not much fault to find in Sonder’s board beyond the standard caveats that an end-grain cutting board requires maintenance in the form of regular oiling and must be hand-washed. The prep grooves are a nice feature, but they aren’t as useful if you’re used to using a bench scraper, since it can’t fit in them. At $179, the Sonder is a bit pricey, but the benefits of end-grain over a cheaper edge-grain board are worth the bump up. If you’re concerned about price primarily, you should opt for the plastic Oxo board recommended below. Because of the carved-in prep containers on one side of the board, you have limited chopping space (but you always have the option to use the other side, which offers a full surface).

What we love: Senior reviews editor, Olivia Tarantino, owns three types of cutting boards (wood, composite, and the MK Midi), and the Midi is the one she grabs for anything short of a full dinner. “It’s closer to midsize than small, which makes it more versatile than a mini board that’s only good for smashing garlic. I can dice a whole onion, slice a tomato, and even fit a mise en place of scallion, ginger, and garlic. Because it’s nonporous, it’s my pick over wood for wetter ingredients, since I can toss it in the dishwasher when I’m done,” she says, noting that she owns the white color and there’s no staining after eight months. The one downside worth noting is that the surface is a bit harder, which can be tougher on knives.

Adding a smaller board like this to a kitchen that already has a large wood cutting board can help for small prep work like slicing fruit, vegetables, or ingredients like garlic without having to clean your substantial board in between.

What we’d leave: We wish that Material would add feet to the larger version of the board. If it’s all you’ve got, a small cutting board can be frustratingly limiting. Also, after years of working with Material’s cutting boards in their homes, our editors noted that they will show visible wear and tear in the form of slice marks and small stains. This is inevitable for any plastic (or similar) cutting board.

Good Grips Plastic Utility Cutting Board.

Industry observers note that what we love: This plastic cutting board from Oxo is very popular in the BA Test Kitchen. It’s budget-friendly and dishwasher-safe and comes with a juice groove. At 14.75" x 10.4", it’s a good size for meal prep, the plastic cutting surface is nonporous, and silicone strips run the length of both short sides to help keep it in place on the counter when cutting. It’s also reversible with one side offering a channel to catch meat juices.

Industry observers note that what we'd leave: The Oxo isn’t very attractive, so you wouldn’t want to use it as a serving board. Also, the longevity of a plastic board like this is only a couple of years, and if you chop too rigorously, the board has been known to shed plastic particles. If you are concerned about plastic use in the kitchen, this isn’t your board.

Yoshihiro Hi-Soft High Performance Professional Grade Cutting Board.

According to recent reports, rubber cutting boards are seen more often in professional kitchens than home ones, but if you’re looking for something large and durable, and you don’t want to have to bust out your knife sharpener regularly, consider this Hi-Soft rubber board by Yoshihiro. It’s very knife-friendly, and cutting on it feels nice. It stays in place on the counter, and unlike another rubber board we tested, it doesn’t have a rubber tire odor.

Sources indicate that what we love: There are a couple of reasons chefs like food-safe rubber cutting surfaces. For starters, because rubber has a little give, the cutting surface flexes ever so slightly to the knife edge versus wearing it down like a hard surface would. Both synthetic and natural rubber are also nonporous, so they’re easier to sanitize than wood boards and are often used by sushi chefs for that reason (conversely, wood cutting boards are actually health-code violations in some cities).

Sources indicate that what we'd leave: Though sanitizing the surface is easy, large rubber boards can be harder to wash because, in addition to being significant, they are also heavier than, say, plastic, and the rubber material must be washed by hand. Rubber cutting boards can also hold on to stains more easily than plastic.

Recent findings suggest that in the long run: With its light color this board has shown a bit of staining and evidence of knife blades running across it. But all things considered, it’s cleaned up very well and proven an excellent companion to an always-out end-grain wood board.

Before getting the knives out, we researched chopping boards and narrowed down a selection that included a wide range of plastic, rubber, and various types of wood boards that ranged from about $10 to almost $300.

To assess the boards’ durability and stability, testers chopped a pound of carrots, diced a large onion, and minced fresh ginger. Testers also cut steamed beets on each board so they could see how much (or how little) each board held on to stains. We chopped lots of garlic on the boards and watched out over the course of the days and weeks of testing for odor retention on the boards. Finally, we washed each board according to the directions and oiled the wood boards that called for it.

Here is an example of the kind of staining you can expect with a wood cutting board. A good scrub with some coarse salt and lemon juice will help take care of this.

These are the qualities we looked for in the best cutting boards.

According to recent reports, we recommend that home kitchens have one large cutting board, ideally around 20" x 15". Additionally, it’s useful to have some supplemental smaller plastic or wood cutting boards (in the 16" x 12" and 12" x 8" ranges) that are easier to transport to the sink for washing or that fit in the dishwasher. You’ll have your bases covered when you have a large board that can take on any large cooking prep task without risk of vegetables flying all over the kitchen, or upon which you can plop a giant piece of meat for carving—but also some small boards that can be used daily for lighter prep, eliminating the need for a daily full-scale clean of your large board.

During testing, I also looked out for board height; if your board is too tall, it adds too much height to the counter, making it awkward for shorter home cooks to get a good angle when cutting. A too substantial or too heavy board is also hard to clean and move.

We recommend rubber, wood, and plastic cutting boards. There’s a trade-off involved in selecting the right hardness level for a cutting board. A material that’s too hard will have you busting out your knife sharpener more often than you should, while a board that’s too soft will end up with cut marks so deep you may no longer have a smooth surface—and it will be harder to clean and sanitize. So you want a durable surface that will feel nice to cut on and have some give. For wood cutting boards, we prioritized boards made with American materials. That’s particularly important because wood sourced abroad is often less sustainably sourced, first because it needs to be shipped overseas, and second because the US has more rigorous forestry regulations than some other countries. For a pro-and-con comparison of the various cutting board materials, scroll farther down the page.

If the board had a special feature, like grippers or a juice channel, we evaluated how functional the features actually were. We measured the amount of liquid the juice grooves held and used any prep compartments.

Chop-N-Slice Series Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board, 18" x 12".

Industry observers note that if you have your heart set on a Boos Board but don’t have a lot of space or want to spend a lot of money, this reversible board from the John Boos Chop-N-Slice series is a high-quality board with a pretty low price tag. It’s made of durable maple wood and arrives oiled (it only barely held on to stains from steamed beets). It’s only 1.25" thick, which contributes to its low price. Though it’s not too big or heavy, it has handle grooves on both ends, which can be helpful if you’re carrying a loaded board. Right out of the box, we felt the board was a little rough, but with a touch of seasoning, it significantly improved.

Rectangular Wood Maple Cutting Board.

This end-grain cutting board was a joy to chop on thanks to its soft and responsive surface—it genuinely felt the best of any of the wood boards we tested. Chopping feels ergonomic and your knife feels protected. The board is also beautiful and would stand proudly in a permanent place on anyone’s kitchen counter. When it arrived, it felt dry and chalky, so it immediately needed to be oiled and treated, whereas the winning end-grain boards felt more ready to go out of the box. And unlike the Boardsmith and Sonder boards, it doesn’t have a juice groove.

Industry observers note that it also seemed slightly uneven or warped from the beginning: The board wobbled back and forth ever so slightly during rigorous chopping, making a slight clanking noise. This was almost imperceptible, and since we’ve used Boos boards over the years and loved their stability and durability, we think it’s likely the flaw of the particular board we tested. So we’d still absolutely recommend Boos end-grain boards.

Large End Grain Prep Station Acacia Wood Cutting Board.

This inexpensive end-grain board comes highly recommended by other review sites, and at $72 at the time of writing, it’s an excellent value for an acacia wood board. Its dark color makes it resistant to showing stains, and after being put through its chopping paces, it had no scratches. However, the board did arrive with a visible scratched-up patch on its lower right corner. Even though it was an end-grain board, I didn’t find it as soft or responsive as the Boos above or either of our winning boards. And the wood isn’t sourced domestically. Still, this is a solid value option.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a large and inexpensive board, this 20" x 15" option from TeakHaus is a good choice. The high-quality edge-grain teak looks great, and the darker wood won’t show stains like lighter-colored wood boards do. Cutting felt comfortable, and one side of this reversible board features a juice groove. It’s an inch-and-a-half tall, and that combined with the size makes it pretty bulky. Also, the smell of ginger lingered on this one a bit after we hand-washed it.

This Kickstarter-funded design isn’t just a cutting board; it’s a whole modular prep station. The cutting board has magnetic sides, onto which snap carved wood prep bowls fitted with stainless-steel containers (or silicone liners, depending on which package you opt for). Those bowls also stack nicely on top of the board for storage, and everything can be arranged and rearranged at the cook’s convenience.

Sources indicate that the design here is clever: It’s satisfying to move the board and containers around because everything fits together in a delightful little puzzle, and attaching the prep bowls produces a satisfying click. The magnetic connection is very secure, and it’s helpful and convenient to have little prep bowls available for sweeping away items as you chop them.

In a recent development, you can select various attachable container sizes, and there’s even a large one that runs the whole length of the cutting board that can be used to set up a dredging station for chicken cutlets. You can also buy lids that fit the containers so that they can go right in the fridge to store leftover prepped items, or sauces you made ahead of time for a dinner party.

Recent findings suggest that we like a lot of what’s going on here, but the board’s edge-grain maple construction doesn’t feel high-quality—it was chalky and rough upon arrival. The system is available in a variety of wood types, so maybe the walnut or Brazilian teak that we didn’t test would fare better. But the system is pricey ($519 for a 13-piece set), and the space you’re offered on the actual cutting surface is limited, so there’s not a ton of room for actual chopping—you dedicate a lot of the counter real estate to the attachable containers. If you’ve been in the market for nice prep containers just as much as you have been for a cutting board and love the idea of a smartly designed holistic system, you’ll like the Chef Station. We love the design in theory, but on the merits of the cutting board alone, it’s not a test winner.

Maple Wood Kitchen Basic Cutting Board.

The JK Adams Maple Wood Basic Cutting Board is made of durable maple. It has a minimal design with no embellishments and won’t add too much height to your prep zone. At just ¾" thick, it’s the thinnest wood board tested. The 17" x 14" footprint also offers a decent amount of space for cutting and chopping but is compact enough to keep in a small kitchen.

Recent findings suggest that the JK Adams Pour Spout Cutting Board stands out because it has a juice groove and a pouring spout on both sides, making it truly reversible for cutting meat. Though this is a sizable board at 20" x 14", the groove and spout do take up a significant portion of the surface area available for cutting, so keep that in mind if you’re looking for something to use for really large cuts of meat. The wood is light-colored and will show stains from something like beets, but keeping it treated with beeswax and mineral oil will provide some stain resistance.

Material Kitchen’s MK Free Board is made entirely of plant-based materials ("100% plant-based biocomposite of natural clay minerals and biodegradable biopolymers," according to Material’s website). That last part is notable—especially if you're concerned about microplastics—because this board has none, hence the name. It's dishwasher-safe and has a loop that makes it easy to pull out of a cabinet or hang from a hook. Overall, it’s a totally fine cutting board you can feel very good about using, but without some plant-based bumpers on the bottom, it won’t get a top spot in our rankings. While the microplastic-free material is wonderful in theory, it feels a bit harder on your knives, and because it doesn't have silicone corners, it’s more prone to sliding around on a quartz countertop. And without anything to soften its landing, the thinner, harder material is also fairly loud.

Silicone Cutting Boards Mats, Set of 3.

Industry observers note that if you’re looking for a nonporous alternative to plastic, rubber is our first pick. But both natural and synthetic rubber cutting boards are pricey, so you might want to consider a silicone cutting board. It’s vital to note that these are mats, not actual boards. But even at ⅛" thick, the material provided a reasonable barrier between the knife and counter. Silicone is flexible so it’s easy to fold into a U-shape to transfer ingredients to a pot or scraps to the trash. These mats are also dishwasher-safe even though they’re very easy to hand-wash. And since the entire mat is silicone, it’s very nonslip. These also have built-in grooves around the entire perimeter and a hole in the corner for hanging and so far, they haven’t held on to any stains (even from steamed beets) or shown any knife marks (even when we tried to make some). That mentioned, some users on Amazon have reported knife damage to their mats, which could be a result of the silicone degrading. Though silicone is durable and heat tolerant, repeated exposure to high heat or sudden temperature changes can weaken its structural integrity, and it can hold on to stains.

The All Aboard cutting board from colorful cookware brand Great Jones is like the original Material reBoard’s bigger, curvier cousin. At 16" x 12", it’s major for a plastic board, and it has a nice loop/handle for hanging. It’s made of BPA-free recycled plastic, and the textured surface is nice to cut on. It doesn't have any sort of silicone grip to keep it in place on the counter when cutting, but it does have a juice groove.

Sources indicate that these double-sided boards come in three sizes; one side has a juice groove and the other has an indentation along the top intended to hold Caraway’s tiny Dot & Dash containers. The boards are made from eco-friendly birch, which is lightweight compared to other woods but feels more like maple when cutting. These boards are also pretty thin, so I have concerns about warping, though limiting exposure to moisture can help with that. The board also comes oiled, though it did hold on to some strawberry and beet stains—as we’d expect any wood board to do.

Architec Original Gripper Cutting Board.

This 14" x 11" polypropylene (plastic) cutting board is fine but nothing special. It comes in a variety of fun colors, it has a handle hole you can use to hang it, and it’s dishwasher-safe. One side has small rubber feet (a.k.a. the “nonslip gripper” base), which does keep the board stationary but also makes it so you can only use one side for chopping.

Epicurean Kitchen Series Cutting Board.

Sources indicate that as much as we love Epicurean’s multipurpose cooking utensil, the brand’s cutting board is a no-go. There’s much to like; the nonporous wood composite is dishwasher-safe and won’t warp or splinter like wood. Plus, it looks so much nicer than plastic. But one reason it’s so durable is that it’s so hard, which made everyone who tried it worry about their knife blades. It was also very loud to use. The pricier nonslip version (which also has a juice groove) was slightly more pleasant to use, but still not recommended.

Sources indicate that at 14.9" x 19.6", this versatile bamboo carving board from Meater (the wireless thermometer brand) offers great surface area. One side is solid and free from embellishments, while the other features a sizable juice groove and pouring spout. But the light-colored wood stained fairly easily in testing and required intense scrubbing after we cut beets on it. And we no longer recommend bamboo cutting boards because the surface is extremely hard on knife edges.

Steelport Steelcore Cutting Board.

Sources indicate that the Steelport Steelcore cutting board is a thin, sexy board from the maker of the also sexy Steelport knives. It’s a dual-sided board; one side is thin, perfectly smooth end-grain walnut, and the other is a durable recycled paper composite material. Embedded between the two is a steel core to prevent the board from warping. The surfaces are incredibly smooth, and the composite side has a juice groove, which maintains the modern look of the end-grain side. Unfortunately, the board we received had hairline cracks which, without the steel core, would have probably knocked three corners off of this board. For such a pricey piece of gear, it wasn’t well-packaged for cross-country transit. But the fact that the board stayed fully intact even with three cracked corners is a testament to the strength of the steel core.

Made In’s tableware, cookware, and kitchen tools have a lot of fans at BA, and I wanted to love Made In’s edge-grain Butcher Block. One side is a solid butcher block surface without any grooves or embellishments, while the other features a juice groove. At 17.75" x 11.75", it’s also a nice size for big cuts of meat or to use as a charcuterie board. Unfortunately, even though it’s “steamed for durability” and appeared to come oiled out of the box, the surface really revealed marks from the chef’s knife we used in testing, and beet juice seeped into and stained the knife marks.

In a recent development, the Totally Bamboo Kauai bamboo board is totally fine. It looks nice enough, it’s lightweight, and it doesn’t stain as easily as other wood cutting boards. But the surface is harder than comparable boards, and in testing, it slid around quite a bit on the counter. It’s also a little high-maintenance for bamboo; you’re supposed to treat it with a food-grade mineral oil every few days for a month, then re-oil “as needed.”.

Sources indicate that the Angled Board from Material, which is generally available in FSC-certified walnut or carbon wood (the latter is actually stained white oak), would certainly make an attractive addition to a modern kitchen. But in testing we found that the smooth laminate coating shows knife marks quite easily. It was also surprisingly slippery when we were cutting vegetables.

Farberware Nonslip Plastic Cutting Board.

Despite its name, the Farberware Nonslip Cutting Board didn’t stay put on the countertop during testing. On the other hand, though it’s not entirely stable, it is a nice size (14" x 10"), and the plastic construction makes it dishwasher-safe.

Nicole Home Flexible Plastic Cutting Board Mats.

Cutting boards (especially plastic ones) have one job, and that is to provide a protective layer between your knife and your counter. These flimsy “cutting board mats” didn’t, well, cut it in that department. They also slid around a lot when we were testing. If pressed, I’d say this type of cutting board (er, mat) could be handy to have around to put on top of a wood cutting board or butcher block countertop to help keep the wood clean and avoid cross-contamination when handling raw meat, but wouldn’t use this for chopping, slicing, or dicing directly on a stone countertop.

The first thing you need to decide on when choosing a cutting board is which material you prefer. Here’s a rundown of what's good and bad about each.

In a recent development, PROS: Plastic cutting boards are useful as a supplement to a larger wooden board because they are lightweight and easy to carry around the kitchen. They are inexpensive, and they can go in the dishwasher. According to food director Chris Morocco, plastic is also a less absorbent material than wood (and about the same as rubber), which means they won’t harbor bacteria as easily. They’re a great choice for cutting raw meat.

It has been revealed that CONS: Plastic boards are harder on your knives than wooden or rubber boards. They will also get dinged up after heavy use, which makes them prone to trapping bacteria. Plastic boards will need to be replaced more often than their wooden counterparts. Some research indicates that microplastics in food could be linked to plastic cutting board use, but the research on the long-term health effects of microplastics remains unclear. You do run the risk of your cutting surface moving around a bit unless you go with one that’s designed to stay put like our top pick here. Chris recommends laying a damp dish towel, paper towel, or nonslip rubber mat under your plastic board to keep it steady. Again, we recommend using your plastic cutting boards supplementally, for less rigorous chopping tasks than your wooden chopping blocks.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: If you’re the kind of home cook who is a dishwasher devotee, isn’t quite ready to invest in a cutting board, or wants to cut up raw chicken one day and mince garlic the next and needs a board that can be a totally clean slate each time, then plastic boards are the pick for you.

PROS: In general, wood is soft enough to protect your chef’s knife but still hard enough for smooth cuts, making it perfect for prepping everything except raw meat, Chris says. (Though you can do that, too, if you’re willing to give them a thorough soapy hand-washing afterward.) Another thing we love about wood boards is that they tend to “heal” themselves (i.e., they close up those knife marks after use), which prevents germ-harboring grooves from forming and keeps them in good shape for longer.

CONS: These boards require the most maintenance because wood is the most absorbent board material out there. They’re prone to retaining odors and stains, which means cleaning and caring for them is extra crucial—and requires more work than plastic or rubber. Scroll to the end for more on how to perform that care. We'll also note that an exception to the “easy on knives” rule is teak, which is a dense hardwood containing silica, a substance known to dull blades. So make sure to check which wood your board is made of, especially because teak boards tend to be less expensive.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Wood boards are best for those who care about beautiful objects and are game to give their kitchenware the care and attention it deserves—you know, the people who are regularly sharpening their knives, maintaining the seasoning on their cast-iron pans, and deep-cleaning their Dutch ovens.

It has been revealed that end-grain wood vs. Edge-grain wood.

Sources indicate that wood cutting boards come in two styles: edge-grain and end-grain. In edge-grain cutting boards, the wood grains are aligned horizontally. In end-grain boards, the wood fibers are aligned vertically. End-grain boards are easier on your knives, because the knife blade slips between the fibers of the board rather than sliding across them. End-grain boards also self-heal better than edge-grain boards, because the fibers can come back together. End-grain boards dry more quickly than edge-grain boards because the individual fibers are more exposed to air. This means they require more regular oiling. However, they are also far less likely to crack than edge-grain boards.

In previous versions of this review, we recommended edge-grain cutting boards because they tend to be less expensive. However, in our most recent update we found plenty of end-grain boards that were within $20 to $30 dollars of their edge-grain competitors. Because the research really reveals that end-grain boards offer better longevity and are better for knife care, we’ve opted to recommend boards only in that style for our top picks this time around. Even if you invest in one that’s expensive (our favorite from Boardsmith), it will last you a very, very with proper care—the cost per use just makes sense.

Rubber cutting boards used to be found only in restaurant supply stores, but they have become more available on the market for regular home cooks in recent years—though they are still as expensive as wood boards.

In a recent development, PROS: The rubber boards were some of our favorites in testing, because the material is so responsive. It’s lovely to slice on this springy surface. Rubber is soft, so it’s extremely easy on knives. The material is also non-porous, and therefore won’t absorb bacteria easily and is scratch resistant. They tend to have slightly textured surfaces, which is helpful for keeping them steady on the countertop. They’re super durable. While they aren’t usually dishwasher-safe, they don’t need any mineral oil applied (unlike wood cutting boards, which do); just wash them with mild detergent and leave them to air-dry.

CONS: The only real cons here are that rubber cutting boards don’t have the luxe look and feel you get from a wood board. They also tend to be heavier and pricier than plastic ones.

There’s a reason these boards are so commonly found in sushi restaurants—the bouncy, softer surface supports a slicing motion rather than a rocking motion, making it optimal for ultra thin-bladed Japanese knives. If you like a heavier Western-style knife and use a rocking motion while chopping, this might not be the right board surface for you. Rubber boards are also quite heavy and difficult to maneuver around the kitchen, and they don’t look as nice as wooden boards.

WHO SHOULD BUY IT: Rubber cutting boards are great for people who like to use Japanese knives and want to invest in a piece of equipment that will last them for years to come, but doesn’t require a whole lot of upkeep.

Cutting board materials we don’t recommend.

How do you clean a plastic cutting board?

As mentioned above, plastic cutting boards are the most low-maintenance option, as you can simply pop (most of) them in the dishwasher. Though, if you’re cutting meat or fish, you need to scrape off any remnants under cold water before throwing it in. In restaurant kitchens, people often have a metal scraper that looks a bit like a palette knife for this; your stainless-steel bench scraper or plastic pastry scraper can also work. It prevents the proteins from cooking into the board’s nooks and crannies in hot water.

How do you clean a rubber cutting board?

Use that same cold water scraping technique if you have a rubber board, then follow with a hot, sudsy soap-up. Both rubber and plastic boards can be left to air-dry because they aren’t prone to warping.

How do you clean a wood cutting board?

Wood cutting boards are a different story than any of the above materials. They’re high-maintenance–but also beautiful, long-lasting, and soft on your chef’s knife. Since you’re using your plastic or rubber board for raw meat (right?), a scrape-down followed by a warm, soapy hand-wash is usually enough for wood boards. Just don’t forget the underside. If you constantly get only one side of the board wet, you are unevenly hydrating the wood. Keep that same idea in mind when cutting: If your board is reversible, try to use both sides of it. If not, chop in different zones of your board to keep the surface evenly worn. That might sound like a lot, but if you chop in the same 2" quadrant daily, the angle on your board will rapidly change, which can cause slippage and, eventually, dull knives. Drying is the last, crucial step. With a clean dish towel, dry your board as thoroughly as possible. Then prop it up on its side until bone-dry to further guard against warping or cracking.

Because knife-friendly wood can harbor bacteria and is prone to staining, an occasional sanitizing session is necessary—and if you are using your wood board for meat, those sessions should be more frequent. Sprinkle any stained areas with coarse salt and rub them with the cut side of half a lemon. To disinfect, dilute some white vinegar with water and spray the surface of your board. Let it sit for a couple minutes before washing and drying. If necessary, you can also sanitize your wood board with a bleach solution, but be sure to dry and then oil it really well after.

POST-CLEANING CARE: Beyond washing, wood boards need to be treated with some TLC. Step right this way for an in-depth explainer on how to clean and care for it, but here’s the gist: At least once a month, pull out a clean microfiber cloth, a food-grade mineral oil, and a food-safe board sealant that combines oil with a protective beeswax. This is just as true if you have an inexpensive teak, acacia wood as it is if you go with something pricier, like a cherry or walnut cutting board.

Recent findings suggest that rub a small bit of the oil onto every surface of your dry, clean board. (You want the board to be really dry before you do this, so as to not seal in moisture.) Follow with the balm, which will buff into a creamy consistency. Don’t wipe that away just yet. Leave your board to deep-condition overnight, and then in the morning, gently wipe away any extra with a cloth or paper towel.

Microfiber Cleaning Cloths, Pack of 12.

Jim Jordan picked as newly introduced minority leader for House GOP

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep.
  • House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a upcoming face atop their ranks, electing Rep.
  • The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, center, arrives for a House Republican leadership candidate forum for the 120th Congress in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday, with Rep. Celeste Maloy, R-Utah, walking alongside him. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

House Republicans on Tuesday opted for a upcoming face atop their ranks, electing Rep. Jim Jordan as the incoming minority leader for the 120th Congress after Republicans suffered massive losses in last week’s midterm elections.

The Ohio Republican defeated outgoing Majority Leader Steve Scalise, R-La., in a closed-door, secret-ballot election. The final tally was 106-73.

“Over the next two years, House Republicans will fight for American families. Democrats offer more government. We will offer more freedom,” Jordan mentioned after the hourslong process.

Sources indicate that the two had been working the phones before making their pitches during a candidates forum in the Capitol Visitor Center’s auditorium on Tuesday morning. Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., announced last week he would not seek a leadership post in the newly introduced Congress, which will be seated on Jan. 3.

“Obviously Jim and I know each other, but I’ve got a proven record of how to bring people together,” Scalise said ahead of the vote, trying to play up his experience, including more than a decade on the leadership team that included a stint as whip.

As House Republicans trickled out of the candidates’ forum for breaks or to take phone calls, one member, granted anonymity to discuss a private session, noted Scalise and Jordan “both have strong points, but they both have flaws.” Each made an unsuccessful bid for speaker in 2023 after the ouster of Kevin McCarthy, before the gavel ultimately went to Johnson.

Declining to reveal which would get his vote, the member mentioned: “I won’t talk about a secret vote, but I know who I think is best to lead us.”.

The incoming minority conference also selected other leaders on Tuesday.

Recent findings suggest that majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota held off a challenge from Texas Rep. August Pfluger to become minority whip in January, despite some grumbling about how tight votes were handled on the floor this year.

“We’ve got to retool our whip operation,” Texas Rep. Nathaniel Moran said Tuesday morning, pointing to “the number of times we were held up by either discharge petitions or failed rule votes.”.

“Those were things that should not have happened in the majority,” remarked Moran as he publicly backed Pfluger for whip.

But Emmer projected confidence after his whip win, comparing the moment to when Republicans were down and out after their losses in 2018 only to rebound a few years later.

“To our colleagues on the left, enjoy this honeymoon phase, because come Jan. 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot,” he mentioned at a news conference, adding that Republicans under his watch would expose the “empty promises” that Democrats made to voters and push back on what he called their “radical” agenda.

According to recent reports, in the day’s only three-way race, conference Chair Lisa McClain of Michigan defeated Reps. Erin Houchin of Indiana and Greg Steube of Florida to keep her spot.

Industry observers note that “We had a spirited leadership election. There were important conversations about the future of our conference, and I listened,” McClain stated at the news conference.

In the race to lead House Republicans’ campaign arm, Rep. Brian Jack of Georgia defeated Rep. Rudy Yakym of Indiana, seen as an up-and-coming Ways and Means Committee member. That means Jack will take on a huge share of the uphill task of selecting candidates and raising funds for the 2028 cycle as he helms the National Republican Congressional Committee.

But most of the attention heading into Tuesday’s closed-door proceedings was on the minority leader race.

In a recent development, johnson, the outgoing speaker, declined to endorse a candidate but had encouraging words for Jordan after his win. “He’s going to do an excellent job. He’s a good, trusted friend and brother,” he said.

In a recent development, rep. Tom Cole, R-Okla., said it was a “tough choice for the conference to make,” but he wasn’t disappointed in the pick. “He was an exceptionally capable chairman of both Oversight and Judiciary. He’s excellent in an interview,” Cole said of Jordan. “He’s got boundless energy and determination.”.

Jordan’s victory means he will form a political and legal tag team with newly installed White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller in pushing back on a number of investigations House Democrats have planned for President Donald Trump, some of his second-term administration officials and his business-minded family members.

Democrats will have more than 250 seats in the chamber, with a number of races still uncalled. Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries of Fresh York, expected to become the next House speaker, told reporters last week he predicts Democrats will have at least 255 seats when all the ballots have been counted and verification processes have played out.

“It’s a historic majority in the 21st century,” Jeffries told reporters in Washington, D.C., the day after the midterms. “The American people have chosen the economy over extremism. The American people have chosen hope over hatred. The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty. The American people have chosen House Democrats because they want to see a dramatic change in direction.”.

Political analysts have predicted an internal battle within the GOP for the direction the party takes over the next two years — and after Trump leaves office in January 2029.

It has been revealed that the Institute for Legislative Analysis, a nonprofit organization that advocates to shrink the size and influence of the government, released a vote study assessment on Monday. Its calculations led ILA to endorse Emmer and three fresh faces: Jordan, Steube and Jack.

Sources indicate that “It’s clear many Republican voters feel their representatives in Washington aren’t representing them,” Ryan McGowan, the institute’s CEO, noted in a statement. “It will be interesting to see whether House Republicans respond by choosing leaders … whose voting records are much more closely aligned with the party’s conservative base.”.

It has been revealed that several GOP sources late last week, granted anonymity to be candid, noted they were expecting a close outcome between Scalise and Jordan, adding Emmer was working the phones hard to remain whip. One said having either Scalise or Jordan atop the conference, with the expectation of Emmer staying on as whip, “won’t be much of a change at the top.”.

Sources indicate that the upcoming leadership team will take over Jan. 3, when Democrats are expected to, in part, use their large majority to target all things Trump 2.0. The same GOP source stated the majority party will “inevitably be pursuing impeachment by August recess despite their disciplined statements to the media pre-election.”.

Trump replied in the affirmative when a “60 Minutes” correspondent asked him in an interview that aired Sunday night if he could work with Democrats, should they also be aggressively investigating his team.

It has been revealed that “Well, I did it for four years,” the president stated of his first term. “They impeached me twice. And there are those that say that worked out to my advantage.”.

Nina Heller, Michael Macagnone and Samantha Freeman contributed to this report.

Industry News: Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (413 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake.
  • Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Recent findings suggest that preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Recent findings suggest that bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

In a recent development, arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

There are few people I trust more in the kitchen than Nigella Lawson. If she told me to put sardines in a birthday cake, I’d believe her. That’s just the kind of culinary authority you earn after nearly three decades of making us hungry through the TV screen. The cookbook author and television personality is now dishing out advice on The Great British Baking Show—she made her debut as a GBBS judge in September—but it’s just a small window into her extensive wisdom.

From the kitchen hacks you’d never expect (like swapping milk for boiling water) to the little techniques that make all the difference in your final bake, this is Nigella Lawson’s best baking advice of all time.

According to recent reports, cooking might not require exact measurements, but baking definitely does. “I think every recipe has to be as precise as possible,” Lawson told Vogue in 2018. “Baking, you have to be really precise. If you’re cooking and it suggests 2 to 3 carrots, it doesn’t really matter because they can be different sizes. It’s not going to alter the taste.”.

Industry observers note that so, you’ve never really baked before. It’s okay to start small! A three-tier chantilly cake your first day in the kitchen probably isn’t your best bet. “It’s vital to go for a simple recipe. Read through the recipe to make sure you understand everything that’s being told to you at the time,” she said. “Look for a recipe that gives you an indication of what to do at each stage. This is what I always say to people: remind yourself you’re not running a restaurant.”.

If you’ve been making your chocolate cake with milk, here’s your sign to stop. Lawson suggests swapping the dairy for hot or boiling water instead to “bloom” the cocoa, dissolve the sugar, and loosen the batter. The result? A crazy moist crumb!

Instead of using plain water when baking bread, Lawson suggests swapping it out for leftover pasta or potato water. “It will help the bread’s texture and rise,” she wrote on X in 2020. “Taste it before adding, though. If very salty, dilute it with fresh water and, obviously, leave any salt in the recipe out.”.

It might sound weird, but Lawson swears by cream of tartar for fluffier, softer scones. “These are the best [ones] I’ve ever eaten, which is quite how it should be since they emanate from one of those old-fashioned cooks who starts a batch the minute the doorbell rings at teatime,” she wrote on her website in 2017. “Yes, I know they look as if they’ve got cellulite—it’s the cream of tartar, which is also why, despite their apparent solidity, they have that dreamy lightness.”.

It has been revealed that lawson’s genius baking hack? DIY self-rising flour. “Nigella tends not to use self-raising flour in her more recent books as she doesn’t bother to keep both plain (all-purpose) and self-raising flour,” her site reads. “Partly because keeping just one type of flour saves on storage space, and partly because if you don’t use self-raising flour regularly, then it will lose its raising power over time.”.

Instead, simply add 2 teaspoons of baking powder for each cup of plain flour. Sift the flour and baking powder together into a bowl before using (and make sure the baking powder is fully integrated), and you’re golden!

Industry observers note that we’re all a little extra busy around the holidays, so if you’re planning a dinner party or holiday get-together, it’s okay to make shortcuts. Even Lawson indicates not everything has to be baked from scratch.

“I have a bit of a weakness for this sort of cake, which is essentially an assembly-job number, a construction of alternate layers of a rich, boozy cream and some store-bought sponge or other,” she told the BBC in 2023 about one of her favorite holiday desserts. “Here the layers comprise a confection of cream and mascarpone, seasonally spiked with Advocaat, full of crystallized ginger, figs and nuts, and that essential component of Christmas: gingerbread.”.

Even Lawson admits: “just the words ‘uniformity of size and shape’ make [her] quake.” Hello, crazy foreshadowing for her future on GBBS.

“I am not in the slightest bit insecure about what I can bake, and I’m so very happy doing it, but shop-bought perfection is way beyond me,” she said in a 2014 interview with The Guardian. “But I’m perfectly content with that, and with the ramshackle homemade-ness of my creations.” If that’s good enough for Nigella, it’s good enough for me!

Can a Pre-Nup Be Romantic?

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (808 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Budgeting, filling out tax forms together, managing family dynamics, and standing in line at city hall: not sexy.
  • It has been revealed that no, the administrative process of a prenup isn’t inherently romantic, and let’s not pretend it is.
  • “I think navigating something that’s challenging in a relationship and coming out of it aligned is romantic, sexy, and empowering,” states Ashley Hesseltine.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Budgeting, filling out tax forms together, managing family dynamics, and standing in line at city hall: not sexy. Not romantic. Alas, they are the mundane mechanics of even the most thrilling of married lives. Soon after a ring is on the finger, many couples are now discussing prenups—and it’s a topic that brings up unglamorous realities.

It has been revealed that no, the administrative process of a prenup isn’t inherently romantic, and let’s not pretend it is. But what it does for the relationship—laying everything bare with radical honesty—is deeply romantic.

“I think navigating something that’s challenging in a relationship and coming out of it aligned is romantic, sexy, and empowering,” states Ashley Hesseltine. The co-host of Girls Gotta Eat spoke openly about choosing to have a prenuptial agreement with her now husband. “But I will not lie. The process of a prenup is inherently annoying, unsexy, and invasive. And it’s admin.”.

Recent findings suggest that wedding planning has a way of sweeping us up into a whirlwind of floral arrangements, seating charts, and linen swatches. Conversations about money, family expectations, and core values naturally come to the forefront next to celebrations.

Luxury wedding planner JoAnn Gregoli agrees that pausing and zooming out to address a prenuptial agreement and the structural foundation of your partnership before you even start picking a venue makes the whole planning process all the more clear. “Marriage isn’t only about romance; it’s also about finances, property, obligations, and decision-making,” she notes. “When a couple confronts the subject together, they feel more like they’re entering the marriage as a team and not as a dictatorship.”.

You’ve likely already experienced that deep feeling of intimacy with your partner after an exceptionally vulnerable conversation with them. This is just like that. Afterwards, wedding planning transforms from a period of financial tension into one of deep alignment.

In a recent development, it helps, but there’s no requirement to execute a 30-page legal document to reap the emotional rewards of the prenup talk. Some value lies in the vulnerability required to have the conversation at all.

Therapist and author Israa Nasir notes that money remains one of the ultimate taboos in modern relationships, often carrying hidden emotional baggage. “Constructive and supportive conversations can reveal parts of yourself that you otherwise might not—deeper insecurities, past experiences with financial trauma, childhood scarcity, and your relationship with money,” she says. “If your partner doesn’t understand why you behave a certain way about money, it’s harder for them to have empathy for you.”.

It may feel like you’re setting up transactional boundaries or betting against your longevity. But in essence, it’s an exercise in radical honesty. Approaching your partner with curiosity rather than judgment is a quick way to turn a wobbly topic fraught with anxiety into a brick in your foundation.

In a recent development, nobody’s excited about asking their partner about student loans or retirement accounts. It may feel daunting. That’s completely normal.

Start small, and don’t put the pressure on this having to be one significant conversation. The first chat can just be about getting their thoughts on prenups in general. Then, you can talk about your thoughts on how you want to manage finances in your relationship. Finally, when you’re ready, you can start diving into assets and what each person wants to walk away with.

The time-old advice of there being no such thing as too much communication stands here. You can even talk about how you want to enter this conversation in a way that might make both of you feel the most comfortable. Agree to enter the discussion with empathy, zero judgment, and positive intent.

Remind yourself that you can frame this discussion around shared goals and mutual care.

Here are a couple of conversation starters:.

I’m fairly certain nobody gets married to get divorced. If it does happen, state laws dictate what happens to you both. Letting state statutes dictate your shared destiny? Not romantic. An act of mutual protection? Maybe even chivalrous.

Sources indicate that family and divorce mediator Aswini Puvitharan highlights how modern prenups are moving away from traditional adversarial mindsets. “Prenups are often introduced as ‘How do I protect what’s mine?’ but the better starting point is ‘What would fairness and financial security look like for both of us?’ The more thoughtful prenups today reflect deep care—providing housing, financial support, or protecting someone who takes a career break to raise children.”.

Sources indicate that protection from potential bitterness or future legal chaos is inherently loving. “It should feel like you and your partner against the prenup, not you and your partner against each other,” says Hesseltine. “It’s an insurance policy you’re probably never going to use, and if you were strong enough to figure this out together in a healthy way, chances are you’ll never need it.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that it is fun to be contrarian.
  • Sources indicate that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop.
  • Industry observers note that you would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that it is fun to be contrarian. I admit to the light thrill it gives me to tell people that I hate oat milk, or that I prefer a wet martini. It’s healthy for all of us to have our preferences. But sometimes what should be a matter of personal taste goes viral, amassing an army of haters who make this preference their entire personality. Think back to the great cake vs. pie wars of the 2010s, when anyone who admitted to liking cake was a tasteless rube. This isn’t even about what you like anymore—it’s about the attention that comes with going against the mainstream.

Sources indicate that this is all to say that complaining about turkey on Thanksgiving has got to stop. It is good, and I need people to stop pretending as if it’s not.

Industry observers note that you would think from the way people talk about turkey around Thanksgiving that a flock of the birds came into their house and killed their mother. In 2020, Business Insider wrote that turkey isn’t good and you should leave it off your Thanksgiving table. Vox insists the (horrifying) numbers of turkeys wasted every year are in service of “a dry, flavorless bird no one likes,” while Milk Street claims anyone who likes it must be “pretending.” Even this very publication called it “The Substantial Freaky Chicken.”.

Respectfully, what on earth are you people talking about? Every year I cannot wait for the unveiling of the turkey. It is the ultimate reminder that this isn’t a normal meal because we do not eat turkey on the regular.

In a recent development, over the years, my family has more often entrusted me with the cooking. We tend to do a version of this Martha Stewart en papillote method and I relish in the work. There is care required to ensure the meat is juicy and golden, and the resulting gravy silky and rich. There is great satisfaction in carrying out the gorgeous centerpiece. There is a subtle butteriness to the meat, and something wilder that even the most factory farmed bird can’t erase. Roasting a chicken is for a Tuesday. Roasting a turkey is for when you have the day off work.

Part of the joy of the turkey, of course, is the leftovers. Turkey congee, turkey pot pie, turkey melts, which will only exist because of Thanksgiving. A feast stretched out, reminding you that abundance does not last for just a day. Do not rob yourself of such plenty.

Obviously, the haters have not stopped millions of turkeys from being served every Thanksgiving. The biggest complaint seems to be that the turkey is never cooked well. And I’ll give you that, with a bigger bird, that you only encounter once a year, it takes planning and effort to ensure the middle doesn’t become a powdery mess while the legs are still raw. But I don’t know, try. There are many things that are tricky to cook that are beloved precisely because of the exhilaration of the challenge, so I don’t know why turkey gets all the heat.

If you’re here, it means you like to cook, even love it, and there are no shortage of recipes guiding you toward bird nirvana. So put your hobby to good use, get a meat thermometer, and figure it out. Because as much fun as it is to be a hater, it’s even more fun to prove everyone wrong with a feast.

BA's Best Orecchiette With Sausage and Broccoli Rabe

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (510 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Epicurious

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero.
  • Recent findings suggest that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work.
  • This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

Recent findings suggest that while orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

Cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

Industry observers note that meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

Add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

According to recent reports, this baked potato stuffed with spinach-artichoke dip is the ultimate solo comfort meal. Classic twice-baked potatoes require two trips to the oven to deliver a pillowy, gussied-up filling and crispy skins all in one bite. Here, I’ve streamlined the workflow with a microwave. By zapping your spuds to start, you can reduce the overall baking time without sacrificing texture. Pick a large russet (or Idaho) for the best results; their relatively high starch and low moisture content helps them bake up airy and light, not gummy.

Sources indicate that the rich, velvety filling that melts over top comes together in moments while your spud cooks. Cream cheese and mozzarella pack in enough dairy richness for a satisfying cheese pull and mellow out the subtle bitterness of baby spinach and nutty tang of artichoke hearts. (It’s vital that your cream cheese is room temperature before you mash it in with the veggies. If it’s still got a chill from the fridge, it won’t fully incorporate.) The Worcestershire sauce is optional, but just a few shakes from the bottle bring instant savory depth to the filling.

It has been revealed that most recipes serve multiple people. In Me, Myself, and Dinner, each dish serves one and only one. That's you! Because whether you live solo (almost 30% of Americans do) or are enjoying a night to yourself, sitting down to a meal should be something to look forward to.

It has been revealed that preheat oven to 425°. Poke 1 large russet potato (about 12 oz.) all over with a fork; rub with avocado or vegetable oil to coat and sprinkle with kosher salt. Microwave potato on a microwave-proof plate on high 5 minutes. Turn potato over and microwave on high until fork-tender, about 5 minutes more. Let potato sit until just cool enough to handle.

While potato is cooling, microwave 5 oz. baby spinach with 2 Tbsp. water in a medium microwave-proof glass bowl until wilted, about 2 minutes. Carefully press leaves to release as much liquid as possible, then drain off liquid. Coarsely chop spinach.

Mix 2 Tbsp. cream cheese, room temperature, in a medium bowl until smooth. Add spinach, 4 quartered artichoke hearts (from a 14-oz. can), coarsely chopped, 2 Tbsp. finely grated Parmesan, 2 Tbsp. coarsely grated mozzarella, ½ tsp. garlic powder, and ¼ tsp. Worcestershire sauce (if using) and fold to combine; season with salt and freshly ground pepper.

Slice potato in half lengthwise and lightly fluff flesh in each half. Set on a small foil-lined rimmed baking sheet. Divide spinach mixture between potato halves, piling high (don’t pack too tightly). Sprinkle more Parmesan over. Bake potato halves until very tender when squeezed and skin is wrinkled and crisp, 20–25 minutes. Let cool slightly before eating.

#54525. Industry News: You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (684 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Delish ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: You May Be Thawing Your Turkey Wrong—Here’s How To Avoid Spreading Salmonella

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (684 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint.
  • According to recent reports, frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option.
  • Sources indicate that making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is a marathon, not a sprint. And the most involved, time-consuming dish is undoubtedly the turkey. The centerpiece of your holiday table needs hours in the oven and at least a day of brining, but don't forget the time it takes to defrost beforehand, too.

According to recent reports, frozen turkeys are generally the more accessible and affordable option. But they do require a little extra TLC and planning. So if you buy a frozen bird this year, you'll need to know how to work with it.

Sources indicate that making sure it tastes good is one thing, but ensuring that it's safe to eat is something else entirely. Like chicken, turkey can spread Salmonella and other harmful bacteria. You should exercise caution at every stage of the process, including thawing, to avoid making your guests sick. Here’s what you should know.

Sources indicate that the USDA says it's also safe to defrost turkey in cold water, but in our opinion, it's not worth the hassle. The best bet is to thaw it in the refrigerator, where the bird can gradually defrost at the safe temperature with less risk of bacterial growth. What you should never do: thaw it on the counter, in the garage, or with warm water.

Industry observers note that these environments are less controlled and can expose the turkey to the temperature danger zone (between 40°F and 140°F), where germs grow rapidly. Even if the center of the turkey is still frozen, the thawed exterior can become a hotbed for Salmonella by the time you're ready to roast.

Recent findings suggest that roasted turkey drippings make great gravy. But raw turkey juice dripping all over your fridge? Not so much. Even shrink-wrapped birds can leak, so you should always store your turkey on a baking sheet or roasting pan while it thaws.

It has been revealed that food safety experts also recommend storing raw meat on the lowest shelf. That way, any leaks are less likely to drip onto other ingredients in your fridge.

Sources indicate that we know you're probably keeping a lot of other ingredients in your fridge, so it can be hard to set aside extra room for the turkey. That said, it's a step worth doing. Giving your turkey plenty of personal space minimizes the risk of raw meat or its juices coming into contact with other ingredients.

Sources indicate that in the event that your turkey does contaminate another ingredient, here's what to know: Foods that won’t be cooked, like salad greens, should be tossed if they’ve come into contact with raw turkey juices. Cooking contaminated foods thoroughly can kill harmful bacteria, but you’ll also need to clean any surfaces the juices touched.

Turkeys are massive, so they take a long time to thaw all the way through. The experts at Butterball say you should allocate a day for every four pounds of turkey if you're keeping it in the fridge. That means if you're working with a 16-pound bird, set aside four days just for defrosting. Once it's fully thawed, Butterball notes your turkey will stay safe in the fridge for up to four days.

According to recent reports, and on top of that, brining can make your turkey even more flavorful. If your frozen bird didn’t come pre-seasoned, consider setting aside another day or two for that step. (Want some guidance? Check out our brining guide.).

It’s extremely important to keep things clean while you’re handling a turkey. One of the most common ways Salmonella spreads in the kitchen is through cross-contamination caused by poor hygiene.

According to recent reports, so wash those hands (including under your fingernails!) with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Make sure you also thoroughly clean any utensils and surfaces that come into contact with raw turkey or its juices using hot, soapy water.

Sources indicate that and above all, don’t stress! Americans prepare millions of turkeys every Thanksgiving, so you're not alone in your turkey-roasting journey. Follow the tips above to ensure yours turns out safe to eat and delicious.

Red-Wine-Braised Short Ribs
