Independents decide the election, again!

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1181 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E.
  • Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep.
  • “We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A group of new senators-elect gather for a photo in Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer’s office in Washington on Monday. The large class of incoming Democratic senators was propelled by votes from independents, Winston writes. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call).

Once more, independents were the decisive factor in what amounts to the Republicans’ midterm disaster that was both broad and deep. No one who reads this column should have been surprised that this growing segment of the electorate became the equivalent of the “deciders-in-chief” who used their vote to send a tough message to the president and his party.

“We hired you to fix the Biden economy and you failed.” Pretty simple.

According to the exit polls, Democrats won independents by an astonishing 22 points. If this holds, it will be the largest margin in the history of exit polling, beating the Republican margin in 2010 of 19 points. For Republicans, this is the fifth consecutive election losing independents.

It was the size of the GOP defeat with independents that put the number of states and congressional districts into play, districts that President Donald Trump won in 2024, many by double digits.

Independents made up 33 percent of the electorate; Democrats were at 35 percent and Republicans at 32 percent. This is the second consecutive election where independents were a larger part of the electorate than one of the major parties. It also reveals that while independents may not have been enthused about voting, they showed up.

Looking at the 13 battleground Senate races, which now include Mississippi, Democrats won independents in all of them by double digits, and 10 of them by 20 points or more. The independent vote allowed Democrats to overwhelm significant Republican Party ID advantages in many red states and districts.

Industry observers note that for example, in Kansas (exit poll not final), Republicans had a 17-point party advantage, but lost independents by 33. Incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall went down with a 5-point loss. In South Carolina, Republicans had a 14-point party advantage, but lost independents by 31 points. A liberal activist Democrat beat a neophyte Republican candidate, appointed Sen. Darline Graham, by 4 points.

According to recent reports, despite Texas Republicans’ 5-point party ID advantage, Ken Paxton lost independents by 31 points and lost the Senate race by a huge 12 points. It goes without saying that voters in Texas shocked Republicans by not only rejecting the president’s primary choice for Senate, but taking down all Republicans in statewide races.

It has been revealed that overall, Republicans lost six states with key Senate races where Trump won by double digits in 2024, with Mississippi being a potential seventh. In the House (with 7 races yet to be called at the time of this writing), Democrats have won 56 congressional districts that Trump carried in 2024, along with carrying all 201 districts that Harris won.

Sources indicate that clearly, Republican operatives, consultants and the media missed the boat when it came to evaluating the viability of House races. Using the 2024 Trump-Harris race results to assess the safety or vulnerability of a particular seat proved to be the wrong context.

It has been revealed that in the spring, I was beginning to see some danger signals in our polling and in public surveys that raised questions for me about just how many House seats were actually in play, fearing perhaps far more than anyone was predicting. By early summer, I decided to undertake a different analysis on the state of current races using the 2020 Trump-Biden results by congressional district. The research found a much larger number of GOP seats could be vulnerable. In the end, the analysis proved to be right. Democrats won all of the 220 districts that Biden carried, and at least 37 seats that Trump won.

Industry observers note that according to the exit polls, the independent vote, not surprisingly, was largely driven by the economy, their top problem concern. Much to the detriment of Trump and the Republicans, 80 percent of independents thought the economy was not good/poor, versus 20 percent who thought the economy was excellent/good. In terms of inflation, 82 percent said it had been a severe or moderate hardship for them, and 89 percent said the cost of living was a crucial or major factor in how they voted for Congress.

The president and his party got the blame. Looking at specific policies, 71 percent of independents thought that Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy, and more broadly, 72 percent said his policies had worsened economic conditions in the country. As a result, Trump’s overall job approval among these voters was 29 percent approve with 71 disapproving; 59 percent strongly disapproving. These extraordinarily bad numbers topped even Biden’s worst job approval numbers.

It has been revealed that trump’s decision to ask voters to “pretend I’m on the ballot,” was, in retrospect, a strategic miscalculation. It was a mistake to tell voters that the economy was in great shape when it was clear the majority of people were very unhappy when it came to inflation — the rising cost of gas and groceries.

A little empathy on economic concerns and a lot better explanation of why the Iran conflict was crucial to national security and worth the economic sacrifice would have gone a long way to minimizing the size of the GOP defeat.

According to recent reports, neither happened, and Republicans were overwhelmed by a blue tsunami almost nobody saw coming. Still, despite the size of the Democrats’ win, they would be wrong to see this as an ideological mandate of any sort. The exit polls showed that the electorate remains center-right. Moderates are the largest component at 41 percent, but conservatives still outnumber liberals by a 33-26 margin.

Independents have a negative view of both parties. Their view of Republicans is 32 percent favorable and 68 percent unfavorable. However, Democrats are not far behind, at 42 percent favorable and 58 percent unfavorable.

According to recent reports, at a policy level when independents were asked which party was better able to handle the economy, 41 percent mentioned the Democratic Party, 28 percent said the Republican Party, and 30 percent said neither. Both parties are well short of a majority. This reflects the fact that the electorate still negatively remembers the Biden economy, but also believes that Republicans didn’t fix it as they promised two years ago.

Democrats would be wise to moderate and not continue down the increasingly extreme progressive path. Republicans and the president need to take a hard look at their own failings and understand that when it comes to voters, especially independents, all the money in the world is no substitute for good candidates with real solutions.

David Winston is the president of The Winston Group and a longtime adviser to congressional Republicans. He previously served as the director of planning for Speaker Newt Gingrich. He advises Fortune 100 companies, foundations and nonprofit organizations on strategic planning and public policy issues, as well as serving as an election analyst for CBS News.

“Chaats are a mighty snack that tell India’s culinary story more adeptly than any other food,” writes Nashville-based Indian chef Maneet Chauhan in her cookbook Chaat. She reminisces about a fruity street snack sold by a chaat vendor near the Hyderabadi train station. Sweet pineapple, tangy lime juice, sour-salty chaat masala, chile powder, cilantro, and pomegranate seeds created what she describes as “a decadent mosaic of colors and plucky flavors.” Chauhan suggests swapping in ripe mango or watermelon when in season, or drizzling the finished dish with lightly salted yogurt for added richness and depth. Serve as a snack, or as a side dish for barbecued meats or seafood.

Few fast food rivalries are as competitive as the battle for the best chicken sandwich. And while plenty of chains have introduced their own versions over the years, Chick-fil-A and Popeyes remain two of the biggest names in the conversation.

In my previous chicken sandwich showdown, I put KFC and Popeyes head-to-head to see which chain served the better sandwich. Popeyes ultimately came out on top, thanks to its bold seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings. This time, I’m putting Popeyes up against one of its biggest competitors: Chick-fil-A.

Recent findings suggest that chick-fil-A has built its reputation around a simple, flavorful chicken sandwich that doesn’t need much to stand out. Popeyes, meanwhile, practically broke the internet when it introduced its now-famous chicken sandwich in 2019, sparking a fast food frenzy.

I ordered each chain’s original chicken sandwich to compare flavor, texture, juiciness, and overall balance. Both have their strengths, but only one can move on as my favorite.

Chick-fil-A’s Original Chicken Sandwich keeps things simple with a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, and a toasted bun.

It has been revealed that chick-fil-A’s chicken is so recognizable for a reason. The seasoning and brine give the fillet a savory, slightly tangy flavor that’s hard to beat, while the crispy breading contrasts nicely with the juicy chicken. The pickles also do their job, adding just enough acidity and crunch to balance out the richness.

Recent findings suggest that my biggest complaint is that I wanted a little more from the sandwich. Compared to other fast food chicken sandwiches I’ve tried, many of which come with some type of sauce, Chick-fil-A’s original feels a bit plain. The chicken has enough flavor to stand on its own, but I think a little mayo or another sauce would have made the overall sandwich even better.

Still, there’s something to be said for a chicken sandwich that relies almost entirely on the quality and flavor of the chicken itself.

According to recent reports, popeyes’ Classic Chicken Sandwich features a breaded chicken fillet, pickles, mayo, and a toasted brioche bun. The sandwich that practically broke the internet when it launched in 2019 still lives up to the hype.

In a recent development, I’ve had this sandwich before where the chicken was slightly dry in spots, but thankfully that wasn’t the case this time. The fillet was juicy, flavorful, and incredibly well-seasoned. The breading had a satisfying crunch, and the bold, savory flavor made me want to keep going back for another bite.

The mayo was another key part of the sandwich, adding a tangy creaminess that complemented the chicken without overpowering it. Paired with the crisp pickles, it helped balance out the richness of the fried fillet.

In a recent development, I also really appreciated the proportions. The soft brioche bun held everything together without overwhelming the chicken, and each bite had a good balance of meat, breading, sauce, and pickles.

Sources indicate that while Popeyes might not always deliver the most consistently juicy chicken, everything came together particularly well during this taste test. Between the seasoning, crispy breading, and well-balanced toppings, it’s easy to understand why this sandwich became such a phenomenon in the first place.

Popeyes already managed to beat KFC in my previous comparison, and after going up against Chick-fil-A, it’s keeping its winning streak alive.

Sources indicate that chick-fil-A arguably has the more distinctive chicken flavor, thanks to its savory, slightly tangy seasoning. But when I’m ordering a chicken sandwich, I want the entire thing to work together, and that’s where Popeyes has the advantage.

It has been revealed that chick-fil-A is still a great option, especially if you prefer a simpler sandwich that lets the chicken do most of the work. But after trying both, Popeyes delivered the better overall experience. With two wins under its belt, Popeyes is proving to be a pretty tough sandwich to beat.

Dirty rice has met its noodle match with our Louisiana-style dirty spaghetti.

Let the good times roll with this Louisiana-inspired dirty spaghetti dish! It’s a riff on Cajun-Creole dirty rice that transforms the original into an easy one-pot pasta.

The key it its flavor is Cajun seasoning, a blend cayenne pepper, garlic powder, black pepper, paprika and thyme. And herein lies an crucial cooking tip: When using store-bought seasoning blends like this one, give them a little taste first before adding anything to the pot. Different brands rely on different ratios of ingredients, and a tablespoon of one product could be much milder (or pack way more heat!) than a tablespoon of another. Your personal preferences matter, too. So whether you are sensitive to spice or like to pack on the heat, make sure you’re adding the proper amount of spice for your taste.

It has been revealed that dirty spaghetti is a riff on dirty rice, a classic Cajun-Creole side dish. Traditional dirty rice is made with chopped organ meats such as chicken livers or gizzards, which, along with the herbs and seasonings, color the white rice and earn it its “dirty” moniker. This dish, however, has a meaty base that’s made with ground beef and diced andouille sausage. Like the original, it also features the “holy trinity” of Cajun and Creole cooking: chopped onion, bell pepper and celery. A healthy dose of Cajun seasoning ensures each bite is packed with bold flavor.

Heat the oil in a large Dutch oven or large high-sided skillet over medium-high heat. Add the ground beef and cook it until it’s browned, four to six minutes, using a wooden spoon or spatula to break it into small crumbles.

Editor’s Tip: If you use a skillet, make sure it has a lid.

Industry observers note that add the chopped andouille sausage, onion, celery, red pepper and green pepper. Cook them until the vegetables are soft, about three to four minutes. Add the garlic and cook it until it’s fragrant, 30 to 60 seconds. Stir in the tomato paste and Cajun seasoning, and cook for one to two more minutes. Add 3 cups of broth and bring the mixture to a simmer.

According to recent reports, add the broken spaghetti to the pot, ensuring that the noodles are submerged in the liquid and separated as much as possible. Add more liquid if needed. Bring the mixture to a boil, then reduce the heat to medium-low. Cover the pot and simmer the pasta for six minutes.

In a recent development, remove the lid and continue simmering until the spaghetti is al dente, stirring every two to three minutes. Add more broth as needed. Remove the pot from the heat, and season the pasta to taste with salt and pepper.

Leftover dirty spaghetti can be stored in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to four days.

In a recent development, the best way to reheat a pasta dish like this one is either in the oven or on the stovetop. To reheat leftover dirty spaghetti in the oven, transfer it to an oven-safe baking dish, cover it tightly with foil, and cook it in an oven preheated to 350 degrees for about 20 minutes or until it’s heated through. To reheat it on the stovetop, heat a saucepan over medium heat and add a drizzle of olive oil. Add the leftover pasta and sauce and saute them for about two to three minutes or until they’re hot.

According to recent reports, yes, you can freeze dirty spaghetti. After allowing it to cool completely, transfer leftovers to a freezer-safe container and store them in the freezer for up to three months. Allow the dirty spaghetti to thaw overnight in the fridge before reheating it.

The best pan for making this one-pot pasta dish is a Dutch oven or a large, high-walled skillet or pot with a tight-fitting lid.

Sources indicate that first, be sure to give your Cajun seasoning a little taste first because seasoning blends like this one can vary widely in spiciness. Depending on how spicy your Cajun seasoning is, add more or less to taste. You could also make a homemade Cajun seasoning blend and customize the amount of cayenne pepper and chili powder to your personal taste. The andouille sausage also adds quite a bit of spice; for less heat, skip it entirely, or swap in sweet Italian sausage, breakfast sausage, chicken sausage or a milder smoked sausage like kielbasa.

Sources indicate that you’ll definitely want to pair this dirty spaghetti with crusty French bread, garlic bread or cornbread to sop up any extra sauce. Southern-inspired side dishes to consider include southern green beans, collard greens or black-eyed pea tomato salad. Or, complement the pasta dish’s spicy flavor with a fresh and crisp green salad.

White House warns Democrats against aggressive oversight

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee.
  • The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.
  • The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., is expected to lead the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

The Trump administration signaled it would respond aggressively to a Democratic-led Congress with a letter this week threatening to prosecute lawmakers for oversight efforts.

The letter from White House Counsel Will Scharf sent Monday to House Oversight and Government Reform ranking member Robert Garcia, D-Calif., argued that members of Congress have limited authority to conduct oversight of a presidential administration and that some of the threats to issue subpoenas “may cross the line into blatant criminality.”.

The letter, obtained from a White House official, marks the latest escalation from the Trump administration ahead of Democrats taking control of both chambers of Congress next year. It also dovetails with years of Trump’s threats to prosecute his critics.

“We are monitoring the abusive and capricious threats that are now proliferating from Democrat legislators who seek to abuse the legislative process to intimidate and to interfere with the lawful functioning of government,” the letter indicates.

Garcia, the likely committee chair next Congress, pushed back on the threat in a statement Wednesday, accusing the administration of having “something to hide” and that Congress has wide authority to investigate the executive branch.

In a recent development, “The American people voted overwhelmingly for us to pass laws to root out corruption and abuse," Garcia said. "The Trump Administration continues to weaponize the government with threats of unconstitutional attacks on Congress. We are a co-equal branch of government and will not be deterred by baseless threats from a weaponized DOJ or from the President’s lawyers.”.

The letter came after Attorney General Todd Blanche previously refused to rule out criminal charges against members of Congress in response to investigations.

"It depends on what the crime is and what they have done,” Blanche told CNN over the weekend.

Last week, President Donald Trump himself noted that threats of investigations and impeachment were “extortion at the highest level” and called for the Justice Department to “look into this criminal act, immediately!”.

He also singled out Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., calling for her to be imprisoned. The administration previously unsuccessfully attempted to indict Slotkin and other Democrats over a video she published calling for soldiers to disobey illegal orders.

And Trump last year publicly called for longtime critic Sen. Adam B. Schiff, D-Calif., to face unspecified charges in a post on Truth Social addressed to then-Attorney General Pam Bondi that also called for the prosecution of former FBI Director James Comey and New York Attorney General Letitia James. Both have faced criminal charges, pleaded not guilty and fought them in court as political attacks.

Industry observers note that garcia and other Democrats have signaled they intend to pursue oversight aggressively in the newly introduced Congress. After Democrats won the House majority last week, Garcia put out an all-caps statement urging administration officials to “LAWYER UP” ahead of the new year.

Garcia, as well as other likely incoming chairs such as House Judiciary ranking member Rep. Jamie Raskin, D-Md.; Homeland Security ranking member Rep. Bennie Thompson, D-Miss.; and Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., have hinted at broad inquiries ranging from the handling of files related to deceased sex offender Jeffrey Epstein to immigration enforcement and more.

Raskin told reporters last week that he thought Democratic oversight efforts could dovetail with the party’s broader effort to address affordability concerns, including by addressing the Iran war, allegations of corruption within the Trump administration and more.

“We're going to get all the information that we need in order to restore the rule of law in American constitutional democracy,” Raskin noted.

The letter also echoes a previous fight the administration pitched with the House in the first Trump administration, where officials resisted in court allowing former White House Counsel Don McGahn to testify to the House Judiciary Committee for years.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

There’s nothing worse than dragging myself out of bed only to realize I’ve run out of coffee beans. That’s where coffee subscriptions come in. But the best services will do more than guarantee you’ll have a consistent supply of freshly roasted coffee—they also let you explore the vast world of coffee. They’re how I’ve discovered some of my favorite roasters, tried single-origins I never would have found on my own, and figured out exactly what I like and don’t like in a cup.

It has been revealed that whether you’re a third-wave coffee nerd looking to try a new craft roaster or a decaf drinker on the hunt for some actually good decaffeinated beans, there’s a subscription for you. After five years of testing, Trade is our top pick—but depending on what kind of coffee you like, I have plenty of other recommendations.

Industry observers note that I know coffee preferences can be wide-ranging, which is why my team and I have scoured the earth for subscriptions that offer tailored picks for different kinds of coffee lovers. To date, we’ve tested nearly two dozen options and recommend the following wholeheartedly.

Fresh in this enhancement: BA editors have been trying out some new deliveries, including some we’re loving from Methodical in Greenville, SC, and Fellow’s Drops program.

Industry observers note that trade is a multi-roaster subscription that sources coffee from independent roasters all over the country. It's great for someone looking for great specialty coffee with an interest in trying a number of different roasters and different roasting styles.

According to recent reports, tester: Chris Morocco, food director This was the easiest subscription I have ever set up, and Trade did such a good job of hitting my preferences right in their sweet spot: medium roast, medium body, medium fruit…just medium all around. I have gotten stuck in the past, tasting the same coffees or coffee styles over and over, and after just two bags, I could tell this would be different.

I set up an order for one 12-oz. bag of whole beans every two weeks. The first bag was Atomic Roasters Space Cadet out of Peabody, MA, and my second bag was Sparrows Coffee, Harmony Series All Seasons Blend from Grand Rapids, MI. I loved the Sparrows bag because it had just enough roast to feel pleasantly dense and weighty on my palate, yet with enough fruit, brightness, and acid to feel lively. When I clicked the box for “medium roast” coffee, this is exactly what I had in mind. I only do pour-over at home, and this was awesome in my Hario V60 coffee dripper.

Recently, senior shopping editor Olivia Tarantino tried Rarities, Trade’s newest program. It’s invite-only, with a rotating lineup of coffees that roasters make as experiments or passion projects. Each coffee is roasted and shipped to order, in batches of a few hundred bags at most. Trade provides detailed instructions direct from the roaster about how to best prepare your beans to get the optimal flavor extraction. She enjoyed an extended fermentation Chiroso variety that had complex acidity of citrus fruits and a slight savory flavor. We haven’t seen anything like Rarities from a subscription service, so serious coffee drinkers should jump on it.

It has been revealed that the bottom line: There is a lot of great coffee in the world, but finding it and getting it right when you want it can be a challenge. Trade takes care of that for you, making this subscription absolutely worth it.

If you’re the kind of person who’s always ordering the fun new seasonal pour-over option at your local craft coffee shop, or who hunts down rare bean varietals like it’s your job, Podium Coffee Club’s Podium Platinum is the coffee subscription for you. Founded in 2023, Podium is a relatively new kid on the block in the world of coffee subs. The concept? A subscription service that solely sends out coffees that have stood on the podium (hence the name) at a major US coffee competition. The brand’s Podium Platinum subscription focuses on coffees that are unique and experimental in some way, be it flavor-wise, varietal-wise, or through the processing technique used.

Testers: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor, and Alaina Chou, commerce writer In the two months we’ve tested this service, we’ve received two bags of coffee that have lived up to that claim. The first bag was a light roast from Royal Flamingo Coffee, a micro-roaster based in Columbus, Ohio. The beans, grown in Colombia, were made using the Black Honey process and mossto lactic fermentation, which you can read more about on Podium’s website. The notes of blueberries, white chocolate, and florals definitely came through in the brewed coffee in both smell and taste, though not too aggressively. We quite enjoyed this one.

The next coffee hailed from Wonderstate Coffee in Wisconsin and claimed notes of gummy bear, melon, and cooked berries. That might seem like a crazy flavor profile for a bag of coffee, but the brewed stuff was subtle and highly drinkable.

Industry observers note that the bottom line: This is a great coffee subscription to get if you’re looking to explore, nerd out on coffee-making processes, or discover award-winning roasters from across the country. Note that Podium also offers a less expensive Podium Gold subscription option, which does not get you the same unique selection that the Platinum offers.

In a recent development, if you’re a curious coffee connoisseur looking to try single-origin coffee from around the world while directly supporting fair trade and sustainable practices, Atlas is the subscription service for you. Every month, you’ll get a bag of single-origin coffee from a different country that comes with an ID card detailing sourcing information and tasting notes.

Industry observers note that tester: Kelly Janke, former director of culinary production The ordering process was easy. It asked me a few questions about my preferences in roast level, brewing type, and coffee quantity, with options ranging from a half bag to four bags per month. The shipping did seem to take longer than I expected, which was my main qualm with the service.

Industry observers note that the beans I received in my first month were medium roast from Rwanda. I really enjoyed the cards that came in the box with tasting notes and information on the growing region. I had chosen two bags per month because I drink a fair amount of coffee, but it’s worth noting that this meant I received two of the same exact coffee (which wasn’t clear at the time of ordering—I had assumed they would be different). I ground the beans in my Oxo burr coffee grinder to a medium grind and brewed them in a Chemex with a metal reusable filter using a 1:16 coffee-to-water ratio. The coffee definitely tasted on the darker side of a medium with notes of grape, red apple, and roasted almonds.

The bottom line: I love to try fresh coffee varieties and appreciate the difference; if you feel similarly, then Atlas is a great option for you.

Sources indicate that if you’ve been reading all of this as a decaf drinker, we have good news for you: there are also some great decaf coffee subscriptions out there, including Swiss Water. This subscription offers a rotating selection of decaf coffees from roasters all across the US, all of which have gone through the Swiss Water process, a chemical-free decaffeination technique that you can read more about here. Note that Swiss Water at the moment only offers whole bean coffees, so you’ll need to grind your own beans if you decide to try it out.

Industry observers note that tester: Alaina Chou I opted for biweekly shipments, though Swiss Water also offers weekly, monthly, and bimonthly. The first coffee I received was from Manzanita Roasting Manufacturer, based in San Diego. There was no informational card included, so all I really gathered about the coffee was that it was from Guatemala and had notes of berries and chocolate, which it did. For a decaf brew, I was impressed by the quality and nuance of the flavor. The same can be said for the second bag of beans I received, which was a blend called Kick Back from South Carolina–based Barista Alley.

The bottom line: You won’t find the kind of customization and curation options here that you see in most of the other subscriptions on this list, but if you’re okay with trying out a range of decaf coffees and aren’t married to one particular roast level or flavor profile, this service will work for you.

Of every coffee subscription we’ve ever tried, this one is unique. Most coffee beans, even if freshly roasted, are stored as green beans for months. Origin Roasted beans hit the roaster almost immediately after harvest and get shipped out right after that. Truly, they are the freshest coffee beans you can get without picking them yourself. It’s a subjective call as to whether that makes the flavor "better," but it makes it different.

It has been revealed that tester: Noah Kaufman Fruity or chocolate tasting notes that are present in beans that sit green are massively accentuated with Origin Roasted beans. If a flavorful cup of coffee is what you’re after, these beans are as flavorful as they come. The brand’s commitment to roasting at the beans’ origin has the added effect of bringing more coffee roasting work and expertise to countries of origin; roasting for most American coffees happens in the United States.

The ordering process is straightforward because there are no choices for you to make. Just give them your address and credit card number, and the coffee will be on its way to you at the end of each month. The firm only sends the beans it is harvesting that month, which come from a single farm somewhere in Central or South America. The locations are limited to ensure that Origin Roasted can actually get the beans to your door while they’re as fresh as they’re supposed to be.

I got beans from all over Central and South America: Guatemala, Nicaragua, Panama, Colombia, Peru, and Brazil. Each coffee was entirely unlike the one that came before it. Shipments only get sent out on the 28th of every month, so I was limited to one bag per month.

Industry observers note that the bottom line: Because of the harvest and roast process, this really is a boutique product, so you can’t order en masse the way you can with larger roasters. I don’t think it makes sense to identify my favorite beans here because you, dear reader, are not guaranteed to get them anyway. What you are guaranteed to get are incredibly cool coffees.

It has been revealed that we are always on the hunt for roasters and subscriptions we haven’t tried. These are the ones that have landed in our grinders recently that we’re loving.

If you're into the idea of coffee drinking as a ritualistic ~experience~, Folk Coffee Club is for you. Founded by a Q-Grader, a.k.a. a sommelier for the coffee world, Folk specializes in rare coffees that score at least 86 points (in Q-Grader speak). Unlike many of the other coffee subscriptions on this list, Folk gives you zero options; instead, they'll send you one shipment every month with two expert-curated coffees.

In a recent development, tester: Alaina Chou What really sets Folk apart, though, are the intentional extras they included with each shipment. Along with the two coffees, each month features a piece of art, a curated playlist, some thought starters, and a tasting guide that elevate the mundane ritual of coffee brewing and drinking into a full-blown experience you're encouraged to slow down and savor. The whole package, coffees included, is meant to draw on a unifying theme.

It has been revealed that folk's first shipment, Volume 00, was titled “Off Script,” and featured two Gesha coffees—a distinctive varietal that takes supreme care to grow. Each coffee tasted unlike any other I've had, one with notes of jasmine and caramelized peach, the other reminiscent of blood orange and dark chocolate. The whole thing was beautifully packaged and felt like a luxurious gift to receive, the thoughtful intention behind each component highly evident.

The bottom line: Think of Folk like a monthly ritual, complete with art, a playlist, and rare coffees you won't find anywhere else. If you're the type to linger over your morning cup, this one's worth every penny.

Sources indicate that there is no better proof point that the world of exquisitely roasted coffee beans has anchored itself absolutely everywhere than the Onyx Coffee Lab. Onyx was started by Jon and Andrea Allen (who would later become a U.S. barista champion) in Springdale, Arkansas, in the Ozarks, and as it has spread throughout the state, it has also become one of the most recognizable names in specialty coffee. Such is Onyx’s reputation that it’s bled over into other areas, landing the Rogers, Arkansas headquarters a nod as a James Beard Award finalist for the best bar program in America.

Sources indicate that tester: Noah Kaufman As for the coffee subscriptions themselves, they’re straightforward to set up: simply tick the box for quantity and the box for frequency. Onyx offers the reliable roaster’s choice option with a lot of interesting single origins and one-offs (I particularly liked a Rwandan washed coffee from Kanzu Station) that all include the most informative explainers I’ve ever seen attached to a bag of coffee. The cards include a breakdown of all the inputs that contribute to the cost, detailed brewing instructions for both pour-over and espresso, and an explanation of the fermentation and roasting process.

For people looking for more familiar flavors, Onyx has subscription options that combine a small amount of more adventurous beans like the Kanzu with its more familiar blends, letting curious drinkers dip their toes in something new. And for a more special experience, Onyx releases a small number of memberships to what it calls “Echelon” for monthly deliveries of its rarest coffee.

Contemporary Coffee Subscription.

Industry observers note that the Greenville, South Carolina roaster has grown now to have five cafes, a robust bakery and tea program, and some of the coolest, most beautiful branding in the coffee world. But it also has a wide range of blends and single-producer beans.

Industry observers note that I first walked into Methodical’s café in Greenville in 2017 for a single origin pour-over, and at the time quick national shipping of fresh coffee was still in its early stages, so that stop didn’t end with me signing up for regular deliveries. But now the infrastructure is there and the coffee is great. Methodical sorts its coffee into three main buckets for three different types of coffee drinkers: classic (where you’ll find medium and dark roasts great for batch brewing and espresso), contemporary (where you’ll find medium roast coffees great for batch brewing or pour-over), and “avant-garde” (where you’ll find lighter roast coffees, sometimes fruity, sometimes tea-like, that are best enjoyed black).

Sources indicate that our editors have used every one of these coffee subscriptions in their homes over several months and some for years. We’ve made sure to try a variety of bean types where possible, and to try the beans with a variety of brewing methods to see how well they perform as espresso, pour-over, drip coffee, and French-pressed coffee.

Our editors are continually testing many of these services and constantly trying new coffee subscriptions to keep this list updated as the market changes, so be sure to check back as we revision it often.

There are hundreds of coffee subscriptions out there, so we followed two guiding principles when selecting which subscriptions to test:.

A coffee’s freshness has a huge impact on its flavor once brewed, no matter if you’re using a fancy espresso machine or a simple French press. The best subscription services will guarantee freshly roasted beans, either roasted to order or within a week or so of shipping.

The other major factor in your coffee’s flavor is how recently the beans were ground. I’m a substantial advocate of ordering whole-bean coffee and grinding the beans just before brewing, so all of the options we tested offer that. (Of course, I know that many people may prefer the convenience of ground coffee. Most of the services below also offer that as an option, although my colleagues and I will continue to raise our eyebrows at you until you get a good coffee grinder.).

Tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor Best for: People who want high-quality coffee, but aren’t interested in choosing from a dizzying array of adventurous options.

Sources indicate that intelligentsia, out of Chicago, is one of the OG players in third-wave coffee (if you’re unfamiliar, "third wave" has a specific meaning, but is sometimes used as shorthand for a generation of coffee roasters deeply invested in quality, consistency, and unique flavors in coffee). Intelligentsia’s House Blend and Black Cat espresso roast have become staples at bakeries and coffee shops all over the country, and its subscription service gives you a regular supply of those two as well as its deeper catalog of different beans. There’s one single origin option, but the subscription itself is mostly based around Intelligentsia’s blends, which rotate seasonally.

Recent findings suggest that this is a pretty simple, straightforward subscription. There is no quiz or process to determine what kind of coffee is “best for you”; rather, you just manually put in which subscription you want, choosing between the same blend (including espresso), rotating blends, or the roaster’s choice. You can also select how many times a month you want beans and how many bags you want per shipment. Changing to a different subscription is also quite easy. While you won’t find the same kind of personalized curation options as some of the other subscriptions on this list, Intelligentsia does offer one of the widest ranges of grind types if you aren’t getting whole bean coffee, running from the finest Turkish coffee grind to a super coarse (even coarser than cold brew) percolator grind.

Sources indicate that I got “Intelligentsia's Choice” because I’m a sucker for single-origin beans (and have had the opportunity to try all their classic blends already). The beans came from some of the strongholds of international coffee production: Ethiopia and Nicaragua. Making a carafe of pour-over coffee a day, enough for two people or one me, I used about one bag every two weeks. The most noteworthy coffee to me was a very fruity natural process Ethiopian coffee. After testing it extensively, I can tell you that this is a reliable, relatively affordable subscription; the Intelligentsia Classics subscription is only $17 a bag. It would be worthwhile for anyone who wants quality but isn’t trying to be too adventurous with their morning coffee.

Just to note, in 2015, Peet’s bought up a majority stake in Intelligentsia. I don’t think it has changed the quality of the coffee at all, but it is something worth being transparent about.

Tester: Carly Westerfield, associate manager of audience strategy Best for: Someone who likes high-quality beans and doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for, but might get overwhelmed by some of the multi-roaster options on this list.

Counter Culture is a longtime favorite roaster of many a BA staffer (food director Chris Morocco included). It has storefronts in several major cities, and you can find Counter Culture’s coffee in stores across the country, but they also offer several subscription options online.

I had a really easy time ordering the coffee. There aren’t endless options to choose from, which is nice because subscriptions like these can sometimes be a lot to manage. Because I wanted to see a variety of beans, there were only two: the Single-Origin Subscription and the Blend Box. I opted for the latter. As someone who’s often overwhelmed by choices, I always appreciate a curated shopping experience where there are fewer things to choose from and therefore fewer things to compare, contrast, and potentially have buyer’s remorse over. I did struggle a little to figure out how to end the subscription; Counter Culture makes that part a little trickier than everything else.

This subscription sends two different blends (12-oz. bags) at a time at a frequency of your choosing. Options there ranged from every week to every eight weeks, and the ability to change this post-purchase was clear. The Blend Box subscription pulls from six blend options ranging from light to dark roast, plus any “seasonal blend’ they have available, so you will end up seeing the same beans after about four deliveries. Shipping was fast and the email communication from CC made it so I always knew when I was being charged and when the box would be shipped and delivered.

While trying out this subscription, I received four different coffee blends: Iridescent Winter Blend, Big Trouble, Fast Forward, and Forty-Six. At home, I use a Moccamaster Thermal Carafe Coffee Brewer and a Baratza Encore Coffee Grinder. With each of the blends I received, I was able to use the same measurements that I always use (9 g of coffee per 6 oz. of water) and found the coffee to be the right strength for me. Each blend has spot-on tasting notes provided as well. Overall, while the flavor profiles were totally different, none were overwhelmingly bitter or acidic—a big no-no in my book. These coffees all had a really well-rounded, almost creamy quality to them that actually resulted in me using way less half-and-half than I normally take in my coffee. By far my favorite blend is, sadly, the limited edition Iridescent Winter Blend. Big Trouble came in a close second.

This subscription is great for someone who likes high-quality beans but doesn’t know exactly what flavor they’re looking for—perhaps, for instance, a recent college grad who’s been drinking coffee for years but hasn’t had to buy it for their own home yet. The ability to pause or change how often the deliveries come also makes it nice for someone who might travel often or need to have more coffee on hand at random times (maybe they have frequent house guests?).

Tester: Maria Paz Mendez Hodes, director of creative development Best for: Eager-to-learn beginners.

Stumptown is a Portland, OR–based roaster that’s been around since 1999. It offers three subscription options: Roaster’s Choice, Blend Shuffle, and Favorite on Repeat. As a novice coffee brewer, I wished there were a little more elaboration on the differences between Roaster’s Choice and Blend Shuffle. In the end I opted for the Roaster’s Choice, which promised to be a tour of seasonal, single-origin, and occasionally rare coffees, changing every two weeks.

I wasn’t 100% sure until the bag showed up at my door that I was ordering whole beans versus ground coffee. To some that may be glaringly obvious, but just another reminder that the site did not seem aimed at rank beginners like me. From what I can tell, Stumptown subscriptions are all whole-bean-only. Beyond that, the ordering process was clear and easy! My first bag arrived three days after ordering, and the next one almost exactly on schedule.

Industry observers note that A guilty confession: We keep breaking the Hario V60 carafe that I use to make pour-over, and I’ve gotten hooked on the extravagant convenience of bottled cold brew. The arrival of the Stumptown beans was exciting enough that we couldn’t wait for a replacement to arrive from Amazon, so we improvised by setting the dripper over a mason jar. Unglamorous setup aside, the first brew was an immediate reminder of the sense pleasures of the morning coffee ritual, dramatically amplified by using the fanciest beans I’d ever purchased. The freshness of the seasonal beans was obvious upon opening the package—they were lustrous and almost oily, with juicy notes that I’ve rarely detected in the supermarket brands near me. I don’t have a highly attuned coffee nose, but I could certainly taste distinct differences between the bags I received: light, bright fruit in the Montes de Oro from Costa Rica and deep caramel and spice in the Duramina from Ethiopia.

Industry observers note that there were blurbs on the back of each bag sketching details about the coffee producers (e.g., how long they’d partnered with Stumptown and some unique features of their agricultural operations). It’s a good initiation for an interested newbie, but I think a coffee enthusiast could still glean quite a bit from these brief details. The one addition I would have loved would have been a card in the box with some deeper insights connecting the tasting notes and flavors to the processes and places mentioned. While there were tasting notes on the website for “Pick of the Week,” the coffee described wasn’t one I had received—another argument for a card in the box.

Tester: Travis Rainey, staff photographer/visuals editor Best for: People who like a little personality in their morning coffee.

In a recent development, I was tempted to choose a curveball and select the espresso subscription, but opted for a more American coffee experience this time. I chose to test the Curated Single Origin subscription, which sends you a different single-origin coffee bean each week. The first bag of beans I received was from Concepción Huista, just north of Huehuetenango in western Guatemala. It was a very light, almost delicate kind of coffee. I had to adjust the grinder setting to a finer coffee ground to make the coffee a little more bold. For the most part, I make coffee with a pour-over method. A newly introduced coffee arrives each week, so the next selection was from Abana Estate near Jimma in southwestern Ethiopia. This has been my favorite coffee to make so far. It's distinctive, spiced, but still goes down smooth. The third variety is Panangan Mata from Aceh on the northern tip of Sumatra in Indonesia. I’ve only had one cup yet, but it’s fruity, which is a fun surprise.

In general, I’ve found that each Equator coffee has had a distinct personality, making this subscription ideal for people who want to have opinions about coffee—the beans here are the kind that sort of demand one of you. I also appreciate that the containers the coffee beans come in feature detailed, but succinct information on where the coffee is coming from.

Tester: Hana Asbrink, deputy food director Best for: Both novice and experienced coffee drinkers alike who want their coffee selections handled for them.

My ordering experience was straightforward. I chose the Roaster’s Choice Subscription, so I didn’t know what I’d be getting first. My first bag (Honduras San Francisco whole beans) had a roast date just three days before it arrived at my house, so you can’t get much fresher than that. I appreciated this first blind bean as I’m not sure I would have chosen it for myself based on my personal preferences. I used a medium grind on the whole beans for my drip coffee maker. I’m curious to see how I’ll enjoy it pulled in the big boy coffee maker as an Americano.

The bag touts tasting notes of strawberry, raspberry, and dark chocolate, which are spot-on. The first whiff gave me a fruit-and-nut chocolate bar, and the taste matches in a delicate way with a touch some floral undertones.

Tester: Carina Finn Best for: Best for someone with a high-end caffeine routine.

You can find a Blue Bottle café in most major cities—the brand makes a reliably great cup of coffee, whether you’re into fruity pour-overs or sophisticated seasonal lattes. Blue Bottle’s coffee subscription makes it easy to recreate that experience at home. It has around 10 different subscription options for things like instant espresso and matcha powders to rotating single-origin offerings and subscriptions tailored to specific roast level preferences.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: Someone looking for seasonality in their coffee.

Recent findings suggest that sightglass is a coffee-shop-slash-roaster based in San Francisco. They offer subscriptions for all of the coffees in their regular lineup if you find a fave you want to stick to, but we’d recommend trying out one of their rotating options to get a taste for all the brand has to offer. That leaves you with either the Blend Shuffle or the Seasonal Variety subscription. The ordering process is simple: Just select which subscription you want, how much coffee you want in each shipment (12 ounces, 2 pounds, or 5 pounds), what kind of grind you want, and how often you’d like to receive deliveries.

Sources indicate that one of the things I like about Sightglass, as opposed to some other coffee shop-roaster hybrids, is that they regularly introduce upcoming single-origin coffees, which might feature in that seasonal subscription. You can also opt in to get notified about any new drops through the Sightglass Batches text-to-order service.

I'm partial to Sightglass’s Blueboon blend. It's a medium roast with notes of milk chocolate, mandarin, and honeysuckle that I quite enjoy brewed as espresso and used in my morning iced latte. It’s beautifully balanced, and the components get changed seasonally to retain the right ratio of sweetness, body, and acidity.

Tester: Alaina Chou Best for: People who want to hone their coffee-tasting skills.

If you dream of being able to approach the coffee world with sommelier-like expertise but you aren’t quite there yet, a Driftaway coffee subscription will help. Driftaway is an immigrant-owned, woman-led roastery based in Brooklyn, NY, and it’s the only service we’ve tried that starts out with a blind tasting. When you go to place your first order, you’ll have the option to choose between light roast, medium, and dark roasts, or espresso (which each include two or three different 4-oz. bags of coffee to blind taste test), or opt for the Explorer Box, which includes five different coffees spanning all roast levels.

If the tasting aspect of this service appeals to you, I’d recommend going with the Explorer Box option. Each initial Explorer Box comes with five mystery coffees, a wheel with flavor notes, a tasting form, and an envelope revealing the identities of your coffees. Driftaway offers weekly virtual tasting classes free of charge, but if you’d rather taste on your own time, they also have prerecorded tasting tutorials available on their website. Regardless of whether you opt for the Explorer Box or a roast-specific subscription, after your initial order, you’ll give feedback on which coffee you preferred in order to inform your future shipments. Many coffee companies even give you the option to send the farmer feedback, which I appreciated.

Along with the Explorer Box, I also tried out the espresso subscription. I was partial to the Burundi Turihamwe and Guatemala Ella blend, which was wonderfully nutty and had notes of milk chocolate and stone fruits. I loved being able to read more about the women farmers behind this blend and trace the story of the coffee from harvest to brewing, a feature that’s in keeping with Driftaway’s overall ethos.

Sources indicate that founded in 2015 in NYC's East Village, Coffee Project NY has grown from a single café into a full operation spanning retail, roasting, wholesale, and education. Owner Chi Sum Ngai is a certified Q grader and roasting championship competitor who personally oversees the roasting program, sourcing from small-scale cooperatives and family farms committed to improving conditions for workers.

Recent findings suggest that tester: Olivia Tarantino, senior commerce editor The subscription is straightforward: select the Roaster's Choice Single Origin Subscription and receive one to three 10-oz. bags one to two times a month. Coffee Project Latest York is not shy about its credentials; each bag arrives with tasting notes, farm sourcing, processing methods, and MASL (metres above sea level, which indicates the altitude at which beans were grown and profoundly impacts flavor). My standout was the Cabra Noir Wush Wush from the Competition Series, a runner-up at Mexico's prestigious AMCCE competition. Produced through anaerobic fermentation, I hand-ground the beans for a Hario pour-over and was met with such vivid guava notes that I double-checked the bag to make sure it wasn't a cofermentation. It wasn't. It was just that good.

Bottom line: Any coffee drinker will appreciate the expertly sourced beans, but this is a subscription where nerds can truly geek out, sampling rare cultivars and competition-level coffees from around the world.

Wonderstate Coffee (Single Origin).

Wonderstate Coffee Blend Shuffle).

Wonderstate Coffee (Roaster's Choice).

A certified B-Corporation with a fully solar-powered roastery, a transparent farmer payment model, and a novel profit-sharing model, Viroqua-based Wonderstate has gained a lot of goodwill for its business practices, but it also makes really good coffee.

It has been revealed that tester: Noah Kaufman Admittedly, this is a bit of a homer pick, as I have long thought Wonderstate to be the preeminent coffee roaster from my beloved home state of Wisconsin. But for those of you not lucky enough to be from Wisconsin, you should get to know them too. Twice named roaster of the year by Roast magazine (which is probably how it ended up as part of the Podium Coffee subscription), Wonderstate regularly has delicious, clean limited edition single origins—I like to get them as part of the single origin flight subscription. The subscriptions themselves come in a few varieties. The single-origin flight delivers three 100-gram packages of Wonderstate’s rarer coffees every two weeks. Roaster’s choice delivers a different single-origin coffee at an interval of your choosing. And the single coffee subscription gives you a regular delivery of the Wonderstate blend of your choosing, if you’re the type who wants more consistency of flavor in your morning cup.

The bottom line: Wonderstate makes excellent coffee and runs an ethical business, which is a combination that's rarer than it should be. If you care about where your money goes as much as what's in your cup, this is the subscription for you.

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Specialty Subscription).

Black & White Roasters (1-Bag Year Round Subscription).

Sources indicate that if you find most black coffee off-putting, you might still love an unadulterated cup from Raleigh, North Carolina’s Black and White Coffee Roasters. Started by two American barista champions, Black and White are masters of the funky and fruity, with lots of experiments in co-fermented coffee (a process that uses actual fruit) and anaerobic fermented coffee (which produces very pronounced fruit notes).

Industry observers note that tester: Noah Kaufman, senior commerce editor It can be a very hands-off subscription. The only required information is whether you want one or two bags at a time and the frequency you need your coffee (anywhere between one and six weeks). Black and White will take care of the rest. If you do see a bag on their website you like, you can add it to your queue; otherwise, the team in North Carolina will select for you.

Every bag I received was of a funky variety, using ingredients like passion fruit, but they produce a number of more classic flavor profiles, which are available as part of their “year-round” subscription; the year-round is also about 20% cheaper than a subscription with the specialty bags.

The bottom line: If you're drawn to funky, fruit-forward coffee but don't want to think too hard about what to order next, Black and White is the subscription for you. Just set your frequency and let the barista champions decide.

Bean Box is focused on the “curation” experience. The service’s tasting team offers what they claim is the largest selection of specialty coffee online, with over 600 different brews in its rolodex. The selection is sourced from dozens of small-batch, sustainably focused roasters from around the country—meaning you could likely go years without tasting coffee from the same roaster twice.

Tester: Dan Siegel, head of video Starting my subscription was exceptionally easy and clear. I appreciated the option to tailor the subscription to my own tastes: Bean Box asked me to choose among Light & Bright, Medium & Cozy, Dark & Toasty, Espresso, or Decaf. For this run, I selected the Curators' Choice option, marketed as the curation team’s seasonal favorites and a mix of latest and old coffees. There is an app available to manage subscriptions and read lengthy details on each roaster or track the origin of your beans.

It has been revealed that this subscription was not designed to save me money on coffee; this is for enthusiasts. My first bag from “Gimme! Coffee,” out of Ithaca, NY, hit hard on the Bean Box mission: The roaster is employee-owned, shipping fair trade beans from Coopfam, Brazil’s first certified fair trade coffee grower. This was a standout for any time of day as a medium-bodied brew, subtly sweet with virtually no bitterness or acidity via my automatic OXO 8-cup machine or my Hario V60 pour-over. My second bag, La Cumbre from Little City in Austin, was a bit too bright and fruity for my taste, advertising caramel, mango, and green apple tasting notes—but this was the path I chose with the Curator’s Choice option.

The bottom line: If you have the means, get the beans. I would keep this going for years if money were no object. The money seems to be going toward roasters that align with my values. One of my values is delicious coffee. But also treating workers at every stop along the way like human beings.

If receiving personalized coffee picks from a catalogue of nearly 600 coffees from 60 different roasters sounds like your cup of tea (or, rather, joe), then I will point you toward MistoBox. I found a lot to love about this service after testing it for several months, particularly the way Misto tailored its selections to me and my taste.

According to recent reports, tester: Alaina Chou, commerce writer The ordering process starts with a quiz covering your preferences: how you take your coffee, roast level, whole or ground beans, and frequency. But what sets MistoBox apart is what comes after: a second, more detailed quiz where you share how you brew, how you grind, and any other specifics to help the team dial in your order. The whole process feels genuinely personal, and that expert-curated aspect is, to me, the other major perk that makes a subscription worth it in the first place.

According to recent reports, I’ve loved every coffee MistoBox has sent me so far. The first shipment was the Roma Espresso Blend from Parisi Artisan Coffee, which was aptly described as having notes of milk chocolate, almond, and honeysuckle. I tend to drink espresso, most often with milk in a cappuccino made using my Breville Oracle Jet. The Roma blend, which MistoBox sent me based on that information, worked beautifully for this.

According to recent reports, after you receive each coffee, you’ll have the chance to rate it out of five and leave any tasting notes, which you can share with your curators if you’d like. Coffees you’ve tried show up in a customer dashboard, as will your “Brew Queue,” a.k.a. the lineup of the next coffees coming to your door. These will appear as “MistoBox’s choice” by default, but if you loved a coffee you tried and want it again, or spy a coffee in their collection that you’d like to request, you can opt to add specific coffees to your queue as well. Anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering upcoming coffees from roasters all over the country will enjoy MistoBox.

The bottom line: MistoBox’s user-friendly interface and extensive feedback options make it a great choice for anyone looking for some expert guidance in discovering upcoming coffees from roasters all over the country.

Are coffee subscriptions worth it?

If you’re a frequent coffee drinker, the answer is probably yes. Whether you have a favorite blend you find yourself buying on repeat or you’re eager to try upcoming beans and hone your tasting skills, a coffee subscription will make your life easier and may even save you some money. If you’re presently buying a bag of beans every few weeks at your local coffee shop or grocery store, that bag could potentially be cheaper when bought on subscription—and you’ll get the added convenience of never needing to worry about restocking your stash.

How do coffee subscriptions work?

Industry observers note that at the most basic level, a coffee subscription works much like any other subscription service: You select a quantity and frequency, and lo and behold, a bag of freshly roasted coffee demonstrates up at your doorstep every one to four weeks, depending what you chose. But no one wants to come home from vacation to a pile of beans that are past their prime, only to receive another package the following day. So these coffee subscriptions make it easy to put your coffee deliveries on hold, or cancel them altogether. Some also offer personalization in the form of quizzes or feedback forms, so you can know you're getting a curated selection that’s tailored specifically to your tastes.

How much coffee should you order?

In a recent development, many of the subscriptions on this list will let you customize your delivery frequency and bag quantity to best accommodate your household size and coffee drinking habits. Ideally, you’ll want to hit a sweet spot where you're using up nearly all of your beans by the time the next shipment comes. Industry News: Keeping the Diwali Flame Burning in Newly introduced York City

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1257 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Saveur

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit.
  • As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood.
  • Industry observers note that in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The akhand diya, the continuously burning flame, has one purpose: to stay lit. It is a small but enduring presence, tended to around the clock, its care passed from one person to the next so that the light never goes out. I’ve often thought about how much of life is like this, how we are constantly passing the torch from one version of ourselves to another.

As a teenager, I remember feeling that I had crossed an invisible threshold into womanhood. I was becoming someone different from the girl I had been, carrying parts of her with me but beginning to understand the world through a new lens. Now, years later, I find myself at another such transition: I am becoming a different version of a woman, one I am still getting to know.

Industry observers note that in many ways, this transition is happening outside of me. Thirteen years ago, I moved away from my family in Mumbai and the home where Diwali had always been celebrated. For all those years, the rituals continued, even as I participated in them from thousands of miles away, mostly over video calls. Back in Mumbai, Diwali meant a house full of family and friends, kitchens bustling with cooking and frying, and the warm glow of diyas illuminating the mandir. I was no longer physically there, but I remained part of it. This year, for the first time, I hosted my parents for Diwali in the home I’ve built for myself in Fresh York City.

According to recent reports, it felt cataclysmic, or at least I was making it feel that way in my head. As I welcomed a different version of myself, I was also taking on a newly introduced role within my family. I was no longer simply the daughter returning to their house for Diwali; I was the one opening my home, preparing the food, tending to the rituals, and making space for the people who first taught me what this celebration means. There is perhaps no greater joy than watching the people I love receive and experience care. And yet, this was a responsibility I had chosen to take on, and one that felt particularly daunting as the eldest daughter. I wanted to get it right.

Recent findings suggest that for me, that care has always found its way to the table. Food is how my family celebrates, how we mark occasions, and, perhaps most importantly, how we look after one another. So naturally, much of my energy went into planning the meal. Despite my best efforts, my dad promptly assigned himself the task of making the goat kari—apparently, even after 13 years away, some things hadn’t changed. We headed to our local butcher in Brooklyn to buy fresh goat meat, and almost immediately, his attention turned to the spice tolerance of my guests.

“How much spice can your friends tolerate?” he kept asking me. “Should I keep it at a level six? But our level six might be their level ten. What do I do?” he lamented. “Relax, they’ll be able to handle it! Just make it our level five,” I told him.

In a recent development, I gave in and handed over part of the kitchen to my mother, too. She took charge of the paneer, cooking generous chunks in a luscious onion-tomato gravy and making the chapatis. Selfishly, I didn’t mind relinquishing that responsibility: This would be my one chance for the year to eat chapatis fresh off the tava, puffed up and piping hot, and made by my mother.

As the days drew closer, I found myself loosening my grip on the plans I’d made. My parents had their own ideas about what needed to be cooked, and while I was initially resistant to them taking over (any immigrant will tell you how hard it is to get our parents to just relax!), I was learning that hosting didn’t necessarily mean doing everything myself. It also meant making room for everyone to contribute and allowing new rituals to form.

Industry observers note that the evening began with freshly fried moong vadas. My mother, of course, insisted on frying them for everyone, right before serving. Made from soaked and ground mung lentils, these little fritters are crisp and golden on the outside, with a soft, almost creamy interior. They have a naturally earthy, nutty flavor from the lentils, sharpened with green chiles, ginger, and spices.

Moong vadas are best eaten immediately, still hot out of the oil, with a tangy green chutney. The scene reminded me of Diwalis back in Mumbai, when the vadas rarely even made it to the serving platter: Everyone would gather around the kitchen, waiting for the next batch to come out of the kadai, reaching for them before they had a chance to cool. I saw the same thing happening in my kitchen in Fresh York.

According to recent reports, in the meantime, my friends Leanne and Christina took charge of the tamarind margaritas, my ode to the soft, sweet-tart tamarind candies I grew up savoring as a kid. The tangy cocktails were a welcome counterpoint to the savory fritters, the perfect way to wake up our taste buds (and made exercising some restraint with those moong vadas before dinner particularly difficult). My brother helped set the table and move furniture around, just as we used to do for our parents back in Mumbai. There was something deeply comforting about watching us fall into these old rhythms.

Industry observers note that the table eventually came together with a mix of dishes that felt both familiar and celebratory. There was chana masala from my cookbook, East to East, alongside my dad’s goat kari, slow-cooked with spices until the meat was tender. My mother’s saucy tomato-onion paneer was accompanied by a pile of chapatis that disappeared almost as swiftly as they came off the stove. We served everything family-style, laying out the dishes on kansa thalis, traditional Indian plates made from bronze or bell metal, an alloy of copper and tin. They reminded me of the way my grandparents served meals, and I wanted to bring a little of that into our Diwali celebration.

At the center of the spread was a vegetable pulao, fragrant basmati rice cooked with carrots, cabbage, cauliflower, and whole spices. Alongside it, I placed bowls of pickled onions and mango achaar, whose sharp, tangy bite cuts through the richness of the karis. There was also cucumber raita, cool and creamy, offering a welcome respite from the heat of the spices. These accompaniments might seem like small additions, but they are essential to the balance of an Indian meal. Every bite can be a little different, depending on what you bring together on your plate.

For dessert, I made homemade gulab jamun, my brother’s favorite. The soft dumplings are made from milk solids and fried until golden, then soaked in a warm saffron-and-cardamom-scented sugar syrup.

Recent findings suggest that as I sat cuddled among both my families, I realized that while it wasn’t the perfectly orchestrated dinner I’d imagined when I first started planning, it was something better. The family I was born into celebrating Diwali alongside the family I’d chosen and built in Fresh York, all gathered around the same table and enjoying every minute of it. Perhaps keeping the flame alive was never about re-creating the past exactly as it was but about allowing it to illuminate whatever comes next.

#54454. Julia Child’s Controversial Thanksgiving Turkey Method Isn’t As Crazy As It Sounds

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (688 w)

Julia Child’s Controversial Thanksgiving Turkey Method Isn’t As Crazy As It Sounds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.
  • In a recent development, julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach.
  • Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Julia Child's solution to a common turkey dilemma was equal parts culinary brilliance and holiday theater.

In a recent development, julia Child had a marvelous way of making even the most intimidating cooking techniques seem entirely within reach. She was a brilliant cook, a gifted teacher, and a woman who understood that a little butter could solve an astonishing number of problems. But perhaps her greatest talent was her willingness to question the rules, even when those rules involved one of America’s most beloved holiday traditions.

Take Thanksgiving turkey. Most of us have spent our lives roasting the bird whole, partly because that’s how it’s always been done and partly because a beautifully browned turkey makes such a magnificent centerpiece on a holiday table. Julia, however, recognized a rather inconvenient flaw in this arrangement: A whole turkey is not well designed for even cooking.

Her solution was ingenious. She took the turkey apart, cooked its individual pieces, and then put the whole thing back together again for presentation. It was a triumph of culinary common sense, with just enough theatrical flair to make the whole thing unmistakably Julia.

It has been revealed that julia called her creation the “re-assembled roast turkey,” a technique she shared in her cookbook, The Way to Cook. Rather than wrestling an entire bird into the oven and hoping for the best, she removed the backbone, separated the leg and thigh portions, and roasted the breast on a bed of stuffing while the dark meat cooked in another pan.

Once everything was properly cooked, she arranged the pieces together on a serving platter, restoring the turkey to something resembling its original form. In her recipe, Julia cheerfully suggested that nobody would ever know the difference.

In a 2012 NPR Thanksgiving segment, Christopher Kimball, who had cooked alongside Julia, demonstrated the method with host Renee Montagne. The two had a wonderful time discussing the reconstructed bird, which they affectionately dubbed “Frankenturkey.” It wasn’t quite traditional, but that was rather the point. Julia had found a way to preserve the spectacle of a whole roasted turkey without actually having to cook one.

Sources indicate that the trouble with roasting a whole turkey is that its various parts have very different needs. The breast is lean and can become dry and stringy when overcooked, while the legs and thighs contain more fat and connective tissue, and generally benefit from cooking to a higher internal temperature. Getting everything just right at the same time is a challenge, even for experienced cooks.

Breaking down the turkey solves much of that problem. With the pieces separated, you can monitor their temperatures individually and remove them as they finish cooking. The dark meat has time to become tender without drying out the breast, and heat circulates more efficiently around the smaller pieces, reducing the overall roasting time.

Recent findings suggest that it’s a method we’ve championed at Taste of Home. Our guide to cooking a deconstructed turkey outlines the process of breaking down the bird, roasting the individual pieces and getting beautifully crisp skin. You can even ask your butcher to handle the disassembly if you’d rather not begin Thanksgiving morning with a pair of poultry shears.

And there’s another advantage Julia certainly appreciated: With the backbone removed, you’ve already got a head start on making a rich turkey stock for the gravy.

Of course, there’s no requirement that you follow Julia all the way through to the reconstruction. You can simply arrange the carved meat on a serving platter and bring it to the table. But I do love that Julia went to the trouble of putting her turkey back together. She understood that Thanksgiving dinner is as much about tradition and presentation as it is about good cooking, and she found a wonderfully clever way to have both.

The result was better-tasting turkey that still got its moment of glory on the table. And if anyone could make taking a turkey apart and putting it back together seem like the most sensible thing in the world, it was Julia Child.
